Stephen's retelling reminds us that human protection is fragile, while God's faithfulness to His people endures beyond any ruler's regard.
7:18.reflection: When human approval or security disappears, where do you turn for your sense of safety?
7:18.action: Memorize or write out one verse about God's enduring faithfulness, and recite it whenever you feel forgotten or overlooked this week.
7:18.prayer: Everlasting God, people forget, positions change, and favor fades—but You never forget Your people. Root my security in Your unchanging care rather than in human approval. Amen.

7:19.devotion: Stephen describes Pharaoh's cruel oppression: treachery against Israel's forefathers and an attempt to destroy their infants. Scripture does not minimize such evil; it names it. Stephen's point is that God's people have faced grave oppression before, and God has responded. This retelling honors the suffering of the oppressed and exposes injustice as opposition to God's purposes.
7:19.reflection: How do you respond when you witness suffering and injustice—do you look away, or bring it honestly before God and act?
7:19.action: Learn about one form of vulnerability facing children or families in your community, and take one practical step to support a ministry or organization serving them.
7:19.prayer: God of justice, You see the suffering of the vulnerable, and You do not look away. Give me courage to name evil honestly, to protect the weak, and to trust Your saving power. Amen.

7:20.devotion: At the very moment of oppression, Moses was born, and Stephen notes he was well pleasing to God. For three months his parents hid him at home, caring for him at great risk. God's deliverer entered the world in the darkest hour, through the quiet faithfulness of a family. Deliverance often begins hidden and small.
7:20.reflection: What ordinary, hidden act of faithfulness might God be inviting from you right now?
7:20.action: Do one quiet, unseen act of care for someone vulnerable today, without seeking recognition for it.
7:20.prayer: Father, You raised up Moses in the very hour of danger, through parents who quietly trusted You. Make me faithful in hidden things, confident that Your timing is perfect even in dark days. Amen.

7:21.devotion: When Moses could no longer be hidden, Pharaoh's own daughter took him in and raised him as her son. The child threatened by the king's edict was nourished inside the king's household. Stephen highlights the irony of God's providence: the oppressor's own house became the shelter of the future deliverer.
7:21.reflection: Where have you seen God use unexpected—even ironic—channels to provide for you or others?
7:21.action: Thank God in writing today for one unexpected person or circumstance He used to provide for you in the past.
7:21.prayer: Sovereign God, nothing is outside Your providence. You turned Pharaoh's household into a refuge for Your servant. Help me trust that You can provide through ways I would never expect. Amen.

7:22.devotion: Stephen, defending himself before the council, reminds them that Moses was raised with every advantage Egypt could offer—educated in its wisdom, capable in speech and action. God prepared His deliverer through unusual means. Moses' Egyptian training was not wasted; it became part of God's design for leading Israel.
7:22.reflection: How might God be using your present circumstances and abilities to prepare you for purposes you cannot yet see?
7:22.action: Write down three skills or experiences you currently have, and ask God to show how He might use them for His purposes.
7:22.prayer: Lord, thank You that no season of my life is wasted in Your hands. Take the abilities and experiences You have given me, and shape them for Your purposes. Help me trust Your preparation even when I cannot see the plan. Amen.

7:23.devotion: Stephen continues his defense by noting that at forty years old, Moses felt a burden rise in his heart to visit his fellow Israelites. Though raised in Pharaoh's household, his sympathies were with God's suffering people. This inward stirring marked the beginning of God's call on his life.
7:23.reflection: When have you felt God stirring your heart toward His people or His purposes, and how did you respond?
7:23.action: Pay attention today to one situation or person God lays on your heart, and take one small step to respond to that burden.
7:23.prayer: Father, tune my heart to Your concerns. When You place a burden for others within me, give me the courage to act rather than look away. Stir in me a love for Your people and a willingness to respond. Amen.

7:24.devotion: Seeing an Israelite mistreated, Moses stepped in and struck down the Egyptian oppressor. Stephen presents this as Moses identifying with his oppressed brethren. While Moses' method was impulsive and would later cost him, his heart to defend the wronged reflected God's own concern for justice and the afflicted.
7:24.reflection: When you witness someone being treated unjustly, is your instinct to look away or to get involved?
7:24.action: If you see someone mistreated today, speak up or seek help for them rather than remaining silent, doing so with wisdom and peace.
7:24.prayer: Lord, You see the oppressed and hear their cry. Give me eyes to notice and a heart that cares. Make me wise and courageous in defending those who are wronged, and keep my zeal grounded in Your justice and peace. Amen.

7:25.devotion: Stephen explains that Moses expected his fellow Israelites to recognize that God would deliver them through him, but they did not understand. Sometimes God's calling on a person's life is misunderstood even by those it is meant to bless. Rejection, however, did not cancel God's plan.
7:25.reflection: Have you ever misunderstood or dismissed someone God was using, or felt misunderstood in your own calling?
7:25.action: Think of someone whose efforts you may have dismissed too quickly, and offer them genuine encouragement or thanks today.
7:25.prayer: Father, forgive me for the times I have failed to see Your hand at work in others. Give me discernment to recognize Your calling in people around me, and patience when my own calling is misunderstood. Your plans stand firm. Amen.

7:26.devotion: The next day Moses returned and tried to make peace between two Israelites who were fighting, asking why brothers should wrong one another. Even after being misunderstood, Moses longed for unity among God's people. Peacemaking is close to God's heart, even when it is hard and unwelcome.
7:26.reflection: Is there conflict among people you care about that God may be inviting you to help reconcile?
7:26.action: If you know of two people in conflict, pray for them both today and, if appropriate, offer a gentle word that encourages reconciliation.
7:26.prayer: God of peace, You call Your children to live as brothers and sisters. Where there is strife among those around me, make me a humble peacemaker. Give me gentle words and a patient spirit, even when my efforts seem unwelcome. Amen.

7:27.devotion: The wrongdoer rejected Moses' intervention, pushing him away and challenging his authority: who made you ruler and judge over us? Stephen points out that Israel often resisted the very deliverers God sent. The pushback Moses faced foreshadowed how God's messengers, including ultimately Jesus, would be refused by His own people.
7:27.reflection: When correction or help comes from an unexpected person, do I receive it humbly or push it away defensively?
7:27.action: Consider whether someone's recent challenge or correction to you might be worth taking seriously, and respond graciously rather than defensively.
7:27.prayer: Lord, keep me from a defensive heart that resists the people You send to help me. Give me humility to receive correction and to recognize Your hand even in unlikely messengers. Soften my heart where it has grown hard. Amen.

7:28.devotion: The offender went further, threatening Moses with exposure of the Egyptian's death. Threats and fear of consequences often silence those who would do good. Moses' secret was out, and his position in Egypt became untenable. Stephen retells this to show that faithfulness to God's people can carry real personal cost.
7:28.reflection: What fears about exposure, rejection, or consequence might be holding you back from doing what is right?
7:28.action: Identify one good action you have avoided out of fear of others' reactions, and take a small, wise step toward doing it today.
7:28.prayer: Father, You know how fear can quiet my voice and slow my steps. Grant me courage to do what is right even when it costs me, and wisdom to act with prudence. Keep me faithful to You above human approval. Amen.

7:29.devotion: Facing rejection and threat, Moses fled to Midian, where he settled as a foreigner and had two sons. What looked like retreat became a season of preparation; decades later God would call him from Midian to deliver Israel. Setbacks in God's story often become the setting for His next chapter.
7:29.reflection: How might your current season of waiting, disappointment, or obscurity be preparing you for what God has next?
7:29.action: Write one way this difficult season could be forming your character, and thank God for it in prayer before bed tonight.
7:29.prayer: Lord, when my plans collapse and I find myself in unfamiliar places, remind me that You are still at work in the waiting. Use this season to shape me, and help me trust Your timing for what lies ahead. Amen.

7:30.devotion: In Stephen's defense before the council, he recounts how Moses, after forty quiet years in Midian, encountered the Angel of the Lord in a burning bush at Mount Sinai. God's timing often includes long seasons of preparation. The wilderness years were not wasted; they were the setting where God chose to reveal Himself and call Moses to his life's work.
7:30.reflection: Where might God be preparing you during a season that feels like waiting?
7:30.action: Identify one area of waiting in your life today and thank God in prayer for the preparation He may be doing there.
7:30.prayer: Lord, help me trust Your timing in the hidden seasons of my life. When waiting feels long, remind me that You are still present and working. Prepare my heart for whatever You are calling me to do. Amen.

7:31.devotion: Stephen continues his account: Moses noticed the burning bush and marveled, drawing closer to see this strange sight. As Moses approached with curiosity, the Lord's voice came to him. Wonder opened the door to revelation. God often meets those who draw near, turning an ordinary moment in the wilderness into an encounter that changes everything.
7:31.reflection: What might God want to show you if you drew nearer to Him with expectant wonder?
7:31.action: Set aside ten quiet minutes today to simply draw near to God in prayer and listen, without rushing.
7:31.prayer: Father, give me eyes to notice Your presence in ordinary places. When You catch my attention, help me draw near instead of hurrying past. Speak to me, Lord, as I approach You with wonder. Amen.

7:32.devotion: The voice from the bush identified itself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the covenant-keeping God of Moses's fathers. Moses trembled and could not look. Standing before the holy God, Moses was reminded that his calling rested on God's ancient promises. God's faithfulness across generations anchors every commissioning He gives.
7:32.reflection: How has God's faithfulness to generations before you strengthened your own trust in Him?
7:32.action: Write down or share one story of God's faithfulness in your family or church history today.
7:32.prayer: God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, thank You for keeping Your promises through every generation. When I stand in awe of Your holiness, remind me that Your covenant love reaches me too. Anchor my faith in Your unchanging faithfulness. Amen.

7:33.devotion: The Lord told Moses to remove his sandals, for the ground where he stood was holy. God's presence made ordinary desert soil sacred. This command invited Moses to approach with reverence and humility. In Stephen's retelling, the moment underscores that encountering God is never casual; His presence transforms common places and calls for humble worship.
7:33.reflection: Do you approach God with reverence, or has familiarity dulled your sense of His holiness?
7:33.action: Begin today's prayers with a deliberate moment of silence, acknowledging God's holiness before presenting your requests.
7:33.prayer: Holy Lord, forgive me when I treat Your presence carelessly. Teach me to come before You with reverence and humility of heart. Make me aware that wherever You meet me becomes holy ground. I worship You today. Amen.

7:34.devotion: God declared that He had surely seen the oppression of His people in Egypt, heard their groaning, and come down to deliver them. Then He sent Moses to Egypt. This verse reveals God's compassionate attention to suffering. He is not distant from the cries of the afflicted; He acts, and He often calls His people to join His work of rescue.
7:34.reflection: Whose groaning around you might God be inviting you to notice and respond to?
7:34.action: Learn about one local ministry that serves people experiencing oppression or hardship, and offer practical help this week.
7:34.prayer: Lord, You see the suffering of the oppressed and hear their cries. Thank You for a God who is not indifferent to pain. Show me how to join Your compassionate work in the lives of hurting people around me. Amen.

7:35.devotion: Stephen highlights an irony: the very Moses the Israelites rejected, asking who made him ruler and judge, became the deliverer God sent. Stephen draws this parallel for his listeners, who had likewise rejected Jesus. God's chosen deliverer was first refused by men, yet God's purpose stood firm through the one they had turned away.
7:35.reflection: Is there someone God is using whom you have been too quick to dismiss?
7:35.action: Consider someone whose gifts or calling you have overlooked, and encourage them personally today.
7:35.prayer: Father, forgive me for the times I have dismissed the people You choose and use. Give me humility to recognize Your work in unexpected people. Help me honor those You send rather than reject them. Amen.

7:36.devotion: Stephen summarizes Moses's ministry: God brought Israel out of Egypt through wonders and signs in Egypt, at the Red Sea, and throughout forty years in the wilderness. The deliverance was God's work from beginning to end, displayed through Moses. Stephen affirms that God's saving power sustained His people across every stage of their long journey.
7:36.reflection: Can you trace God's power sustaining you through every stage of your journey, even the wilderness seasons?
7:36.action: Write a brief timeline of your life marking moments of God's deliverance and provision, then thank Him for each one.
7:36.prayer: Mighty God, thank You for wonders and signs that show Your power to save and sustain. You delivered Your people through the sea and through the wilderness. Deliver me and carry me through every season, I pray. Amen.

7:37.devotion: Stephen reminds the council that Moses himself foretold a Prophet like him whom Israel must hear. In Acts, this prophecy points to Jesus, the greater deliverer. Stephen argues that rejecting Jesus repeats Israel's old pattern of rejecting God's chosen servants. The God who raised up Moses has now raised up Christ, and hearing Him is essential.
7:37.reflection: Is there something Jesus has said that you have been hearers of but not doers of?
7:37.action: Choose one teaching of Jesus from the Gospels today and take one deliberate step to obey it.
7:37.prayer: Lord Jesus, You are the Prophet Moses promised, greater than all who came before. Forgive me when I fail to listen to You. Give me a heart that hears Your word and obeys it faithfully today. Amen.

7:38.devotion: In his defense before the council, Stephen recalls Moses as the one who stood among God's people in the wilderness, mediating the words God spoke at Sinai. Moses received what Stephen calls the living oracles—God's life-giving word—and faithfully passed it on to the people, linking Moses' ministry to the unfolding story of God's revelation.
7:38.reflection: How am I treating God's word as living truth rather than an old, distant document?
7:38.action: Read a portion of Scripture today slowly, asking God to speak through it, and write down one truth to carry into your day.
7:38.prayer: Living God, thank You for speaking and for preserving Your word through faithful hands. Make my heart soft to receive it. Help me treasure Scripture as Your living voice, shaping my thoughts, choices, and love for You and others today. Amen.

7:39.devotion: Stephen reminds the council that their ancestors refused to obey Moses and pushed him away. Though God had delivered them from slavery, their hearts longed to return to Egypt. Stephen's point is that rebellion against God's messengers is an old pattern, and rejection often begins inwardly, in the turning of the heart before any outward act.
7:39.reflection: Is there any place where my heart quietly longs to return to an old way of life that God has delivered me from?
7:39.action: Name one habit or attachment that pulls you backward spiritually, and take one deliberate step today to turn from it toward God.
7:39.prayer: Father, search my heart and show me where I am drifting back toward old bondages You already freed me from. Give me courage to obey Your voice promptly and to follow You forward, even when the wilderness feels long and uncertain. Amen.

7:40.devotion: Stephen continues Israel's wilderness story: when Moses delayed on the mountain, the people demanded that Aaron make them gods to lead them. Because they could not see or control their visible leader, they manufactured something tangible to follow. The passage exposes how impatience with God's timing can push us toward substitute objects of trust.
7:40.reflection: When God seems silent or slow, what do I turn to for comfort and direction instead of waiting on Him?
7:40.action: When impatience rises today, pause and pray briefly instead of immediately reaching for a distraction or quick solution.
7:40.prayer: Lord, You know how quickly I reach for substitutes when You seem slow or silent. Teach me to wait on You with a steady heart. Keep me from trusting things I can see and control more than the God I cannot see. Amen.

7:41.devotion: Stephen describes Israel making the golden calf, offering sacrifices to it, and celebrating what their own hands had made. The tragedy is not only idolatry but misplaced joy—delighting in human achievement rather than in God. This verse invites honest examination of where our celebration and satisfaction truly rest.
7:41.reflection: What work of my own hands am I most tempted to rejoice in rather than rejoicing in God?
7:41.action: Identify one achievement or possession you take pride in, and today thank God explicitly as the giver of every good thing you have.
7:41.prayer: Father, forgive me for the times I have celebrated my own works and forgotten You. Redirect my joy to its true source. Let everything I make and accomplish point back to You, the Giver of every gift, ability, and breath. Amen.

7:42.devotion: Stephen recalls that after Israel's persistent idolatry, God gave them over to further rebellion, citing the prophets' sobering word about empty worship during the wilderness years. The passage shows that persistent unbelief has consequences: God may allow people to follow the desires they have chosen. It is a warning about hardening, meant to awaken rather than despair.
7:42.reflection: Is there a persistent sin I keep excusing that is slowly dulling my sensitivity to God?
7:42.action: Confess one recurring sin to God today in specific words, and ask Him for one practical boundary to help you resist it this week.
7:42.prayer: Merciful God, do not let me drift into hardness of heart. Wake me to any sin I have been excusing, and draw me back with Your kindness. Restore genuine worship to the center of my life, that I may honor You with a sincere heart. Amen.

7:43.devotion: Stephen cites the prophets' indictment that Israel carried idols—images associated with foreign gods—and worshipped what their hands had made, leading to exile beyond Babylon. In context, he shows the council that rejecting God's messengers repeatedly led Israel into idolatry and judgment. The verse calls every generation to guard against quiet, creeping idols.
7:43.reflection: What modern comforts, ambitions, or securities have quietly taken the place in my heart that belongs to God alone?
7:43.action: Take five minutes today to list anything you rely on more than God, then pray over the list, surrendering each item to Him.
7:43.prayer: Lord, expose the idols I carry so easily—ambitions, possessions, approvals, and comforts that compete with You. Uproot them from my heart. Be my first trust and delight, so that my worship is undivided and my hope rests in You alone. Amen.

7:44.devotion: Stephen turns from Israel's failures to God's faithfulness, recalling the tabernacle of witness built in the wilderness exactly as God instructed Moses, according to the pattern he was shown. Even amid human rebellion, God provided a place of His presence among His people, showing that His purposes advance through obedience to His revealed instructions.
7:44.reflection: Am I following God's instructions in my life, or reshaping His patterns to fit my own preferences?
7:44.action: Choose one clear biblical instruction you have been overlooking—such as forgiveness, honesty, or rest—and practice it deliberately today.
7:44.prayer: Faithful God, thank You for dwelling among Your people even when we falter. Teach me to honor Your instructions rather than remaking them to suit myself. Make my life a place where Your presence is welcomed, trusted, and plainly seen. Amen.

7:45.devotion: Stephen traces the tabernacle's journey: the fathers received it, Joshua brought it into the promised land, and God drove out the nations before Israel until David's days. His point is continuity—God's presence and promises moved faithfully through generations. Faithful stewardship means receiving what God has given and carrying it forward obediently.
7:45.reflection: What faith, practices, or responsibilities have been entrusted to me, and how am I carrying them forward for those who come after?
7:45.action: Do one thing today that strengthens your faith for the long haul—such as recording an answered prayer or teaching a truth to someone younger.
7:45.prayer: Lord of every generation, thank You for carrying Your promises faithfully through the years. Help me steward well what I have received, and pass on a living faith to those who follow me, trusting Your presence goes ahead of us all. Amen.

7:46.devotion: In his defense before the council, Stephen recalls David, a man who found favor with God. David longed to provide a permanent dwelling place for the God of Jacob, moving beyond the tabernacle. His desire honored God, even though the task of building the temple would fall to his son.
7:46.reflection: Do I desire to make room for God in my life the way David longed to make room for Him among His people?
7:46.action: Set aside fifteen minutes today to plan one practical way you will give God a settled place in your weekly routine.
7:46.prayer: Father, like David, give me a heart that longs to honor You. Help me delight in Your presence and gladly prepare a place for You in every corner of my life. Amen.

7:47.devotion: Stephen continues Israel's story: Solomon, David's son, carried out the building of the temple. The house was completed, a magnificent center for worship. Stephen acknowledges this faithfully, showing he is not against the temple itself but is about to reframe how his hearers think about God's dwelling.
7:47.reflection: Am I tempted to treat sacred places or routines as if they could contain or control God's presence?
7:47.action: Thank God today, in writing or aloud, for one church, place, or habit that has helped you draw near to Him.
7:47.prayer: Lord, thank You for every place and pattern of worship that has pointed me to You. Keep me grateful for these gifts without mistaking them for You Yourself, who are greater than all. Amen.

7:48.devotion: Stephen makes his crucial point: the Most High God cannot be confined to buildings made by human hands. However glorious Solomon's temple was, it never boxed God in. Stephen's argument, far from blaspheming the temple, echoes Scripture's own teaching about God's transcendence over any earthly structure.
7:48.reflection: Where in my thinking have I shrunk God down to something manageable, familiar, or man-sized?
7:48.action: Write down one area of life where you have assumed God fits your expectations, and intentionally surrender that assumption to Him in prayer.
7:48.prayer: Most High God, forgive me for the times I have tried to keep You small and contained. Enlarge my vision of Your greatness, and teach me to worship You as You truly are. Amen.

7:49.devotion: Stephen quotes the prophet Isaiah, who recorded God's own words: heaven is His throne and earth His footstool. No house people build can be the place of His rest, because He Himself made everything. The Creator of all cannot be housed by His creatures; He graciously condescends to meet with them.
7:49.reflection: How does remembering that heaven is God's throne and earth His footstool change the way I approach worship today?
7:49.action: Step outside at some point today, observe the sky and the earth around you, and let their scale stir reverent worship.
7:49.prayer: Lord of heaven and earth, You rest not because of what I build but because of who You are. Teach me to approach You with humility and awe, worshiping the Maker of all things. Amen.

7:50.devotion: Stephen finishes the quotation: God's hand made all these things. The argument is complete—the temple's builder and the temple's materials both came from God. Humanity gives God nothing He lacks; worship is our glad response to the One who already made and owns everything, not our contribution to His needs.
7:50.reflection: Do I approach worship as something I do for God, forgetting that everything I offer first came from His hand?
7:50.action: Identify one gift, ability, or resource you possess today and consciously offer it back to God in prayer as something that came from Him.
7:50.prayer: Father, everything I have came from Your hand. Free me from pride in what I give or build for You, and let my worship be humble gratitude to the Giver of every good thing. Amen.

7:51.devotion: Turning from history to confrontation, Stephen charges the council with resisting the Holy Spirit, as their ancestors did. Uncircumcised in heart means outwardly religious but inwardly unreceptive. His words are sharp because the stakes are eternal: persistent resistance to God's Spirit hardens people against the very redemption God offers.
7:51.reflection: Is there a prompting of the Holy Spirit in my life that I have been quietly resisting or postponing?
7:51.action: Name one instruction, conviction, or nudge from God you have delayed obeying, and take the first step of obedience today.
7:51.prayer: Holy Spirit, search my heart and expose any hardness in me. Give me soft ears and a willing heart, so that I respond to Your voice with obedience instead of resistance. Amen.

7:52.devotion: Stephen traces a sorrowful pattern: Israel's history included persecution of the prophets who announced the coming of the Just One, the Messiah. Now the council had betrayed and killed that promised One Himself. Stephen is not excusing violence but exposing a long pattern of rejecting God's messengers, culminating in rejecting His Son.
7:52.reflection: When God sends correction or truth into my life through His Word or His people, do I receive it or push it away?
7:52.action: Read one prophetic or corrective passage of Scripture today and ask God to help you welcome its message rather than defend against it.
7:52.prayer: Lord Jesus, Just One, forgive me for the times I have resisted Your truth because it was uncomfortable. Make my heart tender toward Your Word and Your messengers, ready to receive and obey. Amen.

7:53.devotion: Stephen's final point is sobering: the council received the law, tradition says delivered through angels, yet had not kept it. Possessing God's Word is not the same as obeying it. Privilege brings responsibility, and those who know God's law most intimately are most accountable to live it out.
7:53.reflection: Is there a gap between what I know of God's Word and how I actually live it out day by day?
7:53.action: Choose one clear command of Scripture you know well but practice inconsistently, and obey it deliberately at least once today.
7:53.prayer: Father, thank You for the gift of Your law and Word. Keep me from being a hearer only. Close the gap between what I know and how I live, by Your Spirit's power. Amen.

7:54.devotion: Stephen has just finished proclaiming truth about God's faithfulness and Israel's resistance to it. His listeners are deeply convicted, but instead of repenting, their anguish hardens into rage. This verse honestly shows how hearts can respond to conviction with anger rather than humility when truth challenges what we want to believe.
7:54.reflection: When God's truth convicts me, do I soften toward repentance or harden into defensiveness?
7:54.action: When someone's words sting your conscience today, pause before reacting and ask God what He might be showing you.
7:54.prayer: Lord, soften my heart when Your truth confronts me. Keep me from defensive anger, and give me humility to receive correction with grace. Teach me to welcome conviction as Your loving hand at work. Amen.

7:55.devotion: As opposition intensifies, Stephen is filled with the Holy Spirit and granted a vision of God's glory with Jesus standing at His right hand. In his hardest moment, heaven is opened to him. The passage shows God sustaining His witness with a glimpse of Christ's exalted place of honor.
7:55.reflection: Where do I need a renewed awareness of Christ's presence and glory in my own trials?
7:55.action: Set aside five minutes today to simply fix your thoughts on Jesus, praying slowly through who He is.
7:55.prayer: Lord Jesus, when troubles press in, lift my eyes above my circumstances. Fill me with Your Spirit and remind me that You stand honored and exalted, present with me in every hard moment. Amen.

7:56.devotion: Stephen declares aloud what he sees: the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at God's right hand. His confession of Jesus echoes Daniel's vision of the Son of Man. Even under threat, Stephen's testimony points others toward the risen Christ he trusts completely.
7:56.reflection: Would my words point others to Jesus if I were under pressure today?
7:56.action: Share one sentence about what Jesus means to you with someone who would welcome the conversation.
7:56.prayer: Father, give me courage to speak of Your Son openly and graciously. Let my testimony be honest, gentle, and true, so that others might glimpse the glory Stephen saw. Amen.

7:57.devotion: The crowd refuses to hear any more. They shout, cover their ears, and rush at Stephen together. This tragic scene shows how far unchecked anger can carry people, and how truth can be drowned out when listeners refuse even to consider it. Scripture records this without excusing the violence.
7:57.reflection: Am I ever quick to shut out a voice God may be using to reach me?
7:57.action: Practice listening today: before disagreeing with someone, restate their point fairly and consider it prayerfully.
7:57.prayer: Lord, guard me from closing my ears to truth. Give me patience to hear others fully, discernment to weigh what is right, and grace that keeps anger from ruling my responses. Amen.

7:58.devotion: Stephen is dragged outside the city and stoned, a violent mob execution. The witnesses place their clothes at the feet of Saul, a young man approving of this death. Luke's account quietly introduces Saul, whose encounter with Christ will later transform him into a bold apostle of grace.
7:58.reflection: Do I believe God's grace can reach even people who seem far beyond it?
7:58.action: Pray by name today for someone who appears hostile to the faith, asking God to work in their life.
7:58.prayer: Father, You see every person completely, even those who oppose You. I entrust to Your mercy those far from You, remembering how You reached Saul. Let me never write off anyone as beyond Your grace. Amen.

7:59.devotion: As stones fall, Stephen prays, entrusting his spirit to the Lord Jesus. His words echo Jesus' own prayer on the cross. In his final moments, Stephen's faith stays fixed on Christ, showing that communion with Jesus can hold firm even in the greatest suffering.
7:59.reflection: Is my daily walk with Jesus deep enough to sustain me in suffering, not only in ease?
7:59.action: Memorize a short prayer of surrender to Christ and pray it once each morning this week.
7:59.prayer: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit each day I live, not only at its end. Draw me close in ordinary moments so that my trust in You is steady when trials come. Amen.

7:60.devotion: Stephen's dying prayer forgives those killing him: Lord, do not charge them with this sin. Like His Savior, he intercedes for his enemies even as he suffers. Then he falls asleep, a biblical picture of a believer's death as rest. His forgiveness mirrors Christ's own mercy.
7:60.reflection: Who has wronged me that I still need to release into God's hands?
7:60.action: Name one grudge you carry and pray a prayer of forgiveness over that person today.
7:60.prayer: Father, forgive me as You have forgiven me. Give me grace to release those who have hurt me, and let no bitterness take root in my heart. Make me an instrument of Your mercy. Amen.

8:1.devotion: Saul approves of Stephen's death, and a severe persecution scatters the Jerusalem church through Judea and Samaria. Yet this scattering becomes mission: believers carry the gospel wherever they flee, exactly where Jesus said His witnesses would go. God's purposes advance even through the church's suffering.
8:1.reflection: How might God be using a disruption in my life to spread His good news?
8:1.action: Encourage one believer facing hardship today, reminding them God can work through their difficult season.
8:1.prayer: Lord of the church, You work even through persecution and upheaval. Use the disruptions in my life to carry Your gospel further. Strengthen believers who suffer for their faith, and let Your word spread through them. Amen.

8:2.devotion: After Stephen was killed for his faith, devout believers honored him with a proper burial and deep mourning. Their grief was real and expressed openly. Scripture does not rush past sorrow; it shows God's people weeping over loss while still holding fast to their faith and to one another in community.
8:2.reflection: When have I allowed myself, or others, the space to grieve honestly before God?
8:2.action: Reach out today to someone who is grieving; listen, sit with them, or send a thoughtful message of comfort.
8:2.prayer: Lord, You understand our sorrow. Help me to grieve honestly without losing hope, and to comfort others with the same compassion You have shown me. Hold tight all who mourn today. Amen.

8:3.devotion: Saul aggressively persecuted the young church, going house to house and dragging believers off to prison. This sober passage reminds us that following Christ has cost real people dearly, and that even violent opposition cannot stop God's purposes from unfolding.
8:3.reflection: How do I respond when my faith is challenged, misunderstood, or opposed?
8:3.action: Pray today for Christians facing persecution worldwide, and for those who oppose the gospel, as Saul's story later shows God can transform anyone.
8:3.prayer: Father, strengthen my brothers and sisters who suffer for their faith. Guard their hearts, and softening mercy for those who harm them. Keep me faithful when following You is costly. In Jesus' name, Amen.

8:4.devotion: The scattering caused by persecution became the very means of spreading the gospel. Ordinary believers, displaced from their homes, carried the message of Christ wherever they went. What looked like tragedy became mission, proving God's word cannot be imprisoned or silenced.
8:4.reflection: What disruption in my life might God be using to spread His love in a new direction?
8:4.action: Share your faith naturally today with one person—a simple word about what Christ means to you.
8:4.prayer: Lord, You turn setbacks into opportunities for Your gospel. Give me courage to speak of Christ in everyday places, even when life feels unsettled. Use my ordinary moments for Your extraordinary purposes. Amen.

8:5.devotion: Philip, one of the seven chosen to serve, went to Samaria—a place of long-standing tension with the Jews—and preached Christ there. His obedience crossed cultural barriers, showing that the good news is meant for all people, even those we might naturally avoid.
8:5.reflection: Is there a person or group I consider unlikely or uncomfortable to share Christ's love with?
8:5.action: Take a small step across a cultural or social divide today—a kind word, an invitation, or a genuine conversation with someone different from you.
8:5.prayer: Jesus, You crossed every barrier to reach me. Give me courage to move past prejudice and discomfort, to love and share Your truth with people different from me. Amen.

8:6.devotion: When Philip preached in Samaria, the crowds listened attentively and stayed unified, giving weight to what they both heard and witnessed. His message was confirmed by miracles, and the people responded with open hearts. Genuine attention to God's word, accompanied by visible evidence of His power, draws people together and toward Christ.
8:6.reflection: When you hear God's word, do you give it your full attention, or do distractions and doubts crowd it out?
8:6.action: Share something of your faith today with someone receptive, letting both your words and your consistent life back up what you say.
8:6.prayer: Lord, give me ears that truly listen and a heart that responds to Your word. Use my testimony, backed by a changed life, to draw others toward You with one accord. Amen.

8:7.devotion: As Philip preached Christ in Samaria, God confirmed the message with power: evil spirits were driven out, and many who were paralyzed and lame were healed. The passage presents these events as historical acts of God validating the gospel in that city.
8:7.reflection: Do I believe God's power is greater than every brokenness I see around me?
8:7.action: Bring one specific broken situation—yours or someone else's—before God in prayer today, trusting His power and compassion.
8:7.prayer: Almighty God, nothing is beyond Your power to heal and deliver. I bring You the broken places in my life and world. Work according to Your wisdom and mercy, and strengthen my trust in You. Amen.

8:8.devotion: The result of the gospel's arrival in Samaria was great joy throughout the city. When Christ is preached and God's power touches lives, joy follows. This verse captures the gladness of a community transformed by the good news of Jesus.
8:8.reflection: Does my walk with Christ show the kind of joy that would draw others to ask about it?
8:8.action: Express visible joy in Christ today—thank three people for God's goodness in your life or share one answered prayer with someone.
8:8.prayer: Father, fill me with the joy that comes from knowing You. Let that gladness overflow to my family, neighbors, and city, so others may glimpse the goodness of life with Christ. Amen.

8:9.devotion: Simon had practiced sorcery in Samaria and amazed the people, claiming to be someone great. This verse introduces a figure of influence built on self-promotion and the occult, setting up the contrast between human claims to greatness and the true power of God in Christ.
8:9.reflection: Where am I tempted to seek attention or admiration rather than pointing others to Christ?
8:9.action: Examine your motives today: do one good deed secretly, seeking God's approval rather than human praise.
8:9.prayer: Lord, forgive me for the times I crave recognition for myself. Keep me humble, and let every gift and success in my life point to Jesus, the only one truly great. Amen.

8:10.devotion: Everyone in Samaria, from least to greatest, honored Simon, calling him the great power of God. The crowd's admiration shows how easily people confuse spectacle and personality with genuine divine power. True power belongs to God alone, not to impressive human figures.
8:10.reflection: Whose influence am I following most readily—and does it lead me toward Christ or merely toward a personality?
8:10.action: Spend ten minutes today in Scripture, letting God's voice—not the loudest voices around you—shape your thoughts.
8:10.prayer: Father, give me discernment to distinguish human hype from Your true work. Anchor my attention in Your word and in Christ, not in impressive people or personalities. Keep my worship where it belongs. Amen.

8:11.devotion: In Samaria, a sorcerer named Simon had long held the people's attention through his magic. The crowd's loyalty reveals how easily we stay attached to whatever impresses us. They had been amazed for years by spectacle, yet true freedom and wonder were about to arrive through the good news of Christ.
8:11.reflection: What impressive things hold my attention and loyalty more than the Lord does?
8:11.action: Identify one influence or habit that competes for your trust, and take a small step today to loosen its grip.
8:11.prayer: Lord Jesus, forgive me for the times I have been captivated by things that dazzle but cannot save. Turn my eyes toward You, the true source of wonder. Help me give You my full attention and loyalty today. Amen.

8:12.devotion: When Philip preached the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus, the Samaritans believed and were baptized. Unlike their long fascination with sorcery, this was faith in a person and a kingdom. Noticeably, both men and women responded, showing the gospel's reach across the whole community.
8:12.reflection: Is my faith resting genuinely on Jesus Himself, or on things that merely impress me?
8:12.action: Share with one person today something specific you believe about Jesus and why it matters to you.
8:12.prayer: Father, thank You that Your kingdom came near to ordinary people in Samaria and comes near to me. Strengthen my faith in Your Son, and help me live today as a citizen of Your kingdom. Amen.

8:13.devotion: Simon himself believed and was baptized, then continued with Philip, amazed at the miracles and signs he witnessed. His story begins hopefully, yet his amazement centers on the displays of power rather than on the Savior. His example invites us to examine where our wonder truly rests.
8:13.reflection: When I witness God at work, am I amazed at His power or drawn closer to Him?
8:13.action: Spend ten minutes today reflecting on where your sense of awe goes in worship, and gently redirect it to God Himself.
8:13.prayer: Lord, You know my heart better than I do. If my wonder rests on displays rather than on You, lovingly correct me. Teach me to be amazed by Your grace and drawn to Your Son. Amen.

8:14.devotion: When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John. This was remarkable: Samaritans, long estranged from Jerusalem, were welcomed as recipients of God's word. The church responded with care, unity, and personal presence rather than distance or suspicion.
8:14.reflection: Do I welcome fellow believers across old boundaries and differences as the early church welcomed the Samaritans?
8:14.action: Reach out today in a call or visit to a believer whose background or church tradition differs from yours.
8:14.prayer: Father, thank You that Your word crossed ancient barriers and reached those once excluded. Give me a heart that welcomes all Your people, crossing lines of difference with care, unity, and genuine presence. Amen.

8:15.devotion: Peter and John arrived in Samaria and prayed for the new believers to receive the Holy Spirit. Rather than merely inspecting the report, they served it with prayer. Their visit reminds us that spiritual life is God's gift, sought earnestly on behalf of others, not assumed or manufactured.
8:15.reflection: Am I praying earnestly for others to receive and grow in the Spirit's life, or simply assuming they are fine?
8:15.action: Choose one new believer or struggling friend and pray for their spiritual growth aloud today.
8:15.prayer: Holy Spirit, thank You for being God's gift to Your church. Make me someone who prays earnestly for others' spiritual life, not content to assume but willing to seek You on their behalf. Amen.

8:16.devotion: The Samaritan believers had been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, yet the Spirit had not yet come upon them. The text simply describes this transitional moment in the church's early story. It shows that the apostles in Jerusalem kept genuine connection with this new outpost of faith.
8:16.reflection: Do I rely on the Spirit's presence daily, or am I content with outward marks of faith alone?
8:16.action: Begin this morning by consciously inviting the Holy Spirit to guide one specific task or conversation.
8:16.prayer: Holy Spirit, I do not want outward faith alone; I want Your living presence in my ordinary day. Come and fill, guide, and empower me today, and keep my faith inwardly alive. Amen.

8:17.devotion: Peter and John laid hands on the Samaritan believers, and they received the Holy Spirit. The long-divided people of Samaria were knit into the same Spirit-filled family as Jerusalem's church, through the apostles' own ministry. Unity across old hostility became visible and real in this moment.
8:17.reflection: Where might God be calling me to help build visible unity with believers I have kept at a distance?
8:17.action: Take one practical step toward church unity today, such as attending another congregation's service or supporting a joint ministry effort.
8:17.prayer: Lord, thank You that Your Spirit makes one family out of divided people. Heal the barriers in my own heart and life, and make me an agent of Your unity in Your church today. Amen.

8:18.devotion: Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles' hands and offered them money. His old instinct to buy influence resurfaced, treating God's gift as a commodity. The verse warns us how easily self-interest can dress itself in religious clothing, even among those who have believed.
8:18.reflection: Where am I tempted to treat spiritual things as tools for my own status, profit, or influence?
8:18.action: Examine one area where you might be using faith for personal advantage, and confess it honestly to God today.
8:18.prayer: Father, search my motives. Forgive me for the times I approach Your holy gifts with a marketer's heart instead of a worshiper's humility. Purify my desires and teach me to receive Your grace freely. Amen.

8:19.devotion: Simon the sorcerer had believed and been baptized, yet when he saw the Spirit given through the apostles' laying on of hands, he offered money for that power. He still thought of spiritual things as commodities to be bought and controlled rather than gifts freely given by God.
8:19.reflection: Have I ever treated God's gifts as things to acquire for my own advantage rather than treasures to receive humbly?
8:19.action: Identify one area where you've wanted God's power for personal benefit, and confess it honestly to God today.
8:19.prayer: Father, forgive me for the times I've approached You with a consumer's heart. Teach me to receive Your Spirit's gifts with humility, gratitude, and a desire to serve others rather than myself. In Jesus' name, Amen.

8:20.devotion: Peter responds to Simon's offer with sharp rebuke. Grace cannot be purchased. God's gift of the Spirit is freely given to those He chooses, and attempting to buy it reveals a fundamental misunderstanding of who God is and how He works among His people.
8:20.reflection: Where might I be subtly treating my faith as a transaction—trying to earn or trade for God's favor?
8:20.action: Thank God in writing today for one gift of grace you could never earn or repay.
8:20.prayer: Lord, remind me that Your grace is free, never for sale. Free me from thinking I can earn what You give freely. Help me rest in Your generosity with a humble and thankful heart. Amen.

8:21.devotion: Peter tells Simon he has no share in this ministry because his heart is not right before God. This verse reminds us that outward religious participation means nothing if the inner life is misaligned. God looks past appearances to the true condition of the heart.
8:21.reflection: If God examined my heart right now, what would He find there that I've been hiding from others?
8:21.action: Spend five quiet minutes today asking God to search your heart and name honestly what He shows you.
8:21.prayer: Search me, O God, and know my heart. Expose anything within me that is not right in Your sight, and give me the courage to bring it into Your light for healing. Amen.

8:22.devotion: Peter does not leave Simon without hope. He calls him to repent and pray for forgiveness. Even after a serious failure, the door of mercy remains open. Wickedness need not be the end of the story when a person turns back to God in genuine humility.
8:22.reflection: What sin have I been carrying without bringing it to God in honest repentance and prayer?
8:22.action: Set aside time today to confess one specific sin to God and ask Him plainly for forgiveness.
8:22.prayer: Merciful Father, thank You that no failure puts me beyond the reach of Your forgiveness. Give me a repentant heart, and help me turn to You in prayer instead of hiding in shame. Amen.

8:23.devotion: Peter diagnoses the root of Simon's problem: bitterness has poisoned him and iniquity holds him bound. Sin is not merely behavior; it works inwardly, souring the heart and enslaving. Peter names this lovingly, because seeing the disease is the first step toward healing.
8:23.reflection: Is there any bitterness poisoning my heart and quietly shaping the way I think and act?
8:23.action: Name one resentment you've been holding and pray specifically today for God to release you from it.
8:23.prayer: Lord, You see the hidden poisons in my heart. Uproot every bitterness that has taken root in me, and loose me from the sins that bind me. Set me free to love as You love. Amen.

8:24.devotion: Simon's response offers a glimmer of hope. Frightened by Peter's words, he does not argue or bargain. Instead he asks Peter to pray for him. Whatever the full state of his heart, he takes one honest step in the right direction: seeking intercession.
8:24.reflection: When someone confronts my sin, do I get defensive, or do I respond like Simon by asking others to pray for me?
8:24.action: Ask a trusted believer today to pray with you about a struggle you've been facing alone.
8:24.prayer: Father, thank You for the people brave enough to speak truth to me. Give me a soft heart that receives correction well, and help me seek prayer and support instead of hiding my struggles. Amen.

8:25.devotion: After the confrontation with Simon, Peter and John return to their main work: testifying and preaching the word of the Lord. On their journey back to Jerusalem, they share the gospel in village after village of Samaria, showing how the good news spreads through ordinary faithfulness.
8:25.reflection: Am I sharing my faith in the ordinary, everyday places of my life, or only when circumstances feel dramatic?
8:25.action: Look for one natural opening today—a conversation, a need, an encouragement—to share something of your faith with someone.
8:25.prayer: Lord, make me faithful in the small, ordinary moments. Use my everyday words and actions to carry the good news of Jesus to the people You place along my path. Amen.

8:26.devotion: God directs Philip to a desert road heading toward Gaza. It seems like an unlikely assignment—an empty stretch of wilderness. Yet God is preparing a divine appointment there, and Philip's willingness to go where he is sent becomes part of a much larger story of the gospel spreading.
8:26.reflection: When God's direction in my life seems impractical or confusing, do I trust Him enough to obey anyway?
8:26.action: Practice simple obedience today: do one thing you sense God prompting you to do, even if it seems small or odd.
8:26.prayer: Father, help me trust Your guidance even when Your path seems strange or the road feels empty. Give me the readiness of Philip, who arose and went without needing to understand everything first. Amen.

8:27.devotion: Philip obeys the Spirit's direction and meets an Ethiopian official on the desert road. This man holds high responsibility over the queen's treasury, yet he has traveled a great distance to worship in Jerusalem. His journey shows a heart genuinely seeking God, even from a distant land.
8:27.reflection: When has God's prompting to go somewhere or speak to someone seemed inconvenient, and how did you respond?
8:27.action: Ask God today to make you alert to one person He may want you to approach, then take the first step.
8:27.prayer: Lord, give me Philip's willingness to rise and go. Help me notice the seekers You place in my path today, and make me ready to serve them with a glad and obedient heart. Amen.

8:28.devotion: The Ethiopian is journeying home, but the worship he sought has left him with questions. He fills the miles by reading Isaiah the prophet aloud from his chariot. God is already working in his heart through Scripture before any human messenger arrives.
8:28.reflection: What Scripture are you reading right now, and are you letting it raise honest questions in your heart?
8:28.action: Carry a Bible passage with you today, on paper or phone, and read it during an empty moment.
8:28.prayer: Father, thank You that Your Word travels with me. Use my reading to stir hunger for You, and prepare my heart for whatever understanding You intend to give. In Jesus' name, Amen.

8:29.devotion: The Spirit speaks a simple, specific instruction: go near and overtake the chariot. Philip's earlier obedience positioned him for this moment. This verse reminds us that evangelism in Acts is Spirit-led, not a human strategy, and that guidance often comes one clear step at a time.
8:29.reflection: Are you listening for the Spirit's voice in the ordinary moments of your day?
8:29.action: Pause two or three times today to pray briefly, "Lord, what do You want me to do next?"
8:29.prayer: Holy Spirit, tune my ears to Your gentle directions. Give me courage to act promptly on Your promptings, even when they seem small or unexpected. Lead me to the people You are already preparing. Amen.

8:30.devotion: Philip runs to the chariot and hears the Ethiopian reading Isaiah aloud. He opens the conversation with a respectful question about understanding rather than a speech. Asking good questions opens doors; Philip meets the man where he is and invites honest conversation about God's Word.
8:30.reflection: Do you tend to talk first and listen later, or do you ask questions that show genuine interest?
8:30.action: Begin a spiritual conversation today by asking a sincere question instead of offering an immediate answer.
8:30.prayer: Lord Jesus, teach me to ask kind, honest questions that open hearts rather than close them. Help me listen well before I speak, trusting You to guide the conversation. Amen.

8:31.devotion: The eunuch admits he cannot understand Isaiah without a guide, and he invites Philip to sit with him. Humility like this is a great gift. God often works through willing teachers and willing learners, and honest admission of need is where real understanding begins.
8:31.reflection: Who has God provided in your life to help you understand His Word more deeply?
8:31.action: Invite someone to read Scripture with you this week, whether a friend, family member, or small group.
8:31.prayer: Father, give me the eunuch's humility to admit what I do not understand, and Philip's patience to guide others gently. Make me both a willing learner and a faithful teacher of Your Word. Amen.

8:32.devotion: The eunuch is reading Isaiah's famous passage about a silent, suffering servant led like a sheep to slaughter. In Acts, Philip will explain this as fulfilled in Jesus. The verse shows how Old Testament prophecy points to Christ, and how God prepared this seeker's questions in advance.
8:32.reflection: How does Jesus' willing, quiet suffering for our sake shape the way you see His love for you?
8:32.action: Read Isaiah 53 today slowly, noting each phrase that reminds you of Jesus, and thank God for each one.
8:32.prayer: Lord Jesus, You were led like a lamb without resisting, bearing what we could not bear. Deepen my gratitude for Your willing sacrifice, and help me trust You in my own sufferings. Amen.

8:33.devotion: The passage continues with the servant's humiliation: justice denied and life taken from the earth. Philip later shows the eunuch that this describes Jesus, who was wrongfully condemned yet entrusted Himself to God. His unjust suffering becomes the very means of salvation for all who believe.
8:33.reflection: When you face unfair treatment, what would it look like to entrust yourself to God rather than retaliate?
8:33.action: If you are nursing a grievance today, write it down, pray over it, and choose to release it to God.
8:33.prayer: Father, You watched Your Son suffer injustice without opening His mouth in defense. Teach me to entrust myself to You when I am wronged, trusting Your justice instead of my own. Amen.

8:34.devotion: The eunuch asks the crucial question: is Isaiah speaking of himself or someone else? His honest inquiry gives Philip the opening to share the good news about Jesus. A sincere question, asked from a seeking heart, can become the doorway through which salvation enters a life.
8:34.reflection: What lingering question about faith have you been afraid to ask, and to whom could you bring it?
8:34.action: Write down one honest question you have about Scripture or faith, and bring it to a mature believer or pastor this week.
8:34.prayer: Lord, thank You that honest questions honor You. Give me courage to ask what I wonder, and readiness to answer others' questions with gentleness, as Philip did, pointing always to Jesus. Amen.

8:35.devotion: Philip met an Ethiopian official reading Isaiah aloud in his chariot. Rather than keeping distance, Philip drew near, began at that very Scripture, and explained how it pointed to Jesus. Honest, patient conversation about Scripture opened the door for the gospel to reach a seeking heart.
8:35.reflection: Whom might God be inviting me to walk alongside and point gently toward Jesus?
8:35.action: Offer to listen to a friend's spiritual questions today, sharing your faith warmly without pressure or argument.
8:35.prayer: Lord, thank You that Scripture leads us to Jesus. Give me courage like Philip, a listening ear, and the right words when You open a door for me to share Your good news today. Amen.

8:36.devotion: As Philip and the Ethiopian traveled together, they came upon water along the road. Hearing the good news of Jesus, the official's heart responded immediately: he wanted baptism. His eager question shows how understanding the gospel creates a longing to respond to God's grace right away.
8:36.reflection: How readily do I respond when God stirs my heart to take a step of faith?
8:36.action: Notice one prompting from God today and respond promptly instead of postponing it.
8:36.prayer: Father, You make seeking hearts find the way. Keep my heart tender and quick to obey when You call me, so I never let delay cool what Your Spirit has kindled. In Jesus' name, Amen.

8:37.devotion: When the eunuch asked about baptism, Philip named the one requirement: wholehearted belief in Jesus. The man confessed plainly that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. Salvation rests not on status, ritual, or ancestry, but on sincere personal faith in Christ, openly declared.
8:37.reflection: Do I believe with all my heart that Jesus is the Son of God, and does my life say so?
8:37.action: Take a quiet moment today to reaffirm your faith in Jesus aloud or in writing.
8:37.prayer: Lord Jesus, Son of God, I believe in You. Strengthen my faith where it wavers, deepen my conviction, and help me confess You freely with both my words and my life. Amen.

8:38.devotion: The chariot stopped, and Philip baptized the Ethiopian official in the water beside the road. This simple, joyful act publicly marked the man's new identity in Christ. Baptism pictured his entrance into the faith, welcoming one whom many would have considered an outsider into God's family.
8:38.reflection: How do I treat fellow believers who seem different from me—am I truly welcoming?
8:38.action: Reach out warmly today to a believer whose background differs from yours, welcoming them as family.
8:38.prayer: Gracious God, thank You that Your family crosses every boundary human eyes draw. If my baptism marked my belonging to You, help me live it out by welcoming others as You welcomed me. Amen.

8:39.devotion: After the baptism, the Spirit carried Philip away, and the eunuch never saw him again. Yet he went on his way rejoicing. The new believer did not depend on Philip's continued presence; he left with joy, carrying the gospel home in his own heart and story.
8:39.reflection: Does my joy rest on circumstances and people, or on Christ Himself?
8:39.action: Write down one reason you have to rejoice in the Lord today and thank Him for it.
8:39.prayer: Father, thank You that the joy You give travels with us wherever we go. Let my rejoicing rest in Christ alone, steady when people and places change, and overflowing to those around me. Amen.

8:40.devotion: Philip reappeared at Azotus and continued north through city after city, preaching the gospel until he reached Caesarea. The evangelist who had gone to the desert road simply resumed the work wherever God placed him, showing a life shaped by ready obedience rather than grand strategy.
8:40.reflection: Am I willing to serve God faithfully in the ordinary places my daily life takes me?
8:40.action: Look for one simple opening today—at work, home, or errands—to encourage someone with your faith.
8:40.prayer: Lord, make me faithful in the in-between places, not only the memorable moments. Wherever You set me down today, help me live and speak so that others hear of Your Son. Amen.

9:1.devotion: Luke now introduces Saul as a fierce opponent of the church, breathing threats against the disciples of the Lord and seeking authority from the high priest. The narrative honestly records persecution in progress; the story that follows will reveal how radically God's grace can transform even a persecutor.
9:1.reflection: When I face hostility to my faith, do I trust God with the situation instead of retaliating?
9:1.action: Pray today for one person who opposes or misunderstands Christian faith, asking God to work in their heart.
9:1.prayer: Lord Jesus, even Your enemies were not beyond Your reach. When I face hostility, guard me from bitterness and fear. Help me pray for those who trouble Your people, trusting You with the outcome. Amen.

9:2.devotion: Saul asked the high priest for letters authorizing him to arrest followers of the Way in Damascus and bring them bound to Jerusalem. His zeal was real, but aimed at the wrong target. Scripture here shows how sincerely misplaced conviction can wound others—an ancient scene, a lasting caution.
9:2.reflection: How can I make sure my strong convictions are shaped by truth and love rather than blindness?
9:2.action: Before acting on a strong opinion today, pause and ask whether it reflects Christ's love and humility.
9:2.prayer: Father, You know how conviction can go astray. Search my heart, correct my blindness, and make my zeal for You flow through truth, humility, and love for the people around me. In Jesus' name, Amen.

9:3.devotion: Saul was traveling to Damascus to arrest believers when a sudden light from heaven surrounded him. This moment interrupted a journey of hostility and began one of Scripture's most dramatic encounters with the risen Christ. God can break into our plans, even the ones headed in the wrong direction.
9:3.reflection: Where might God be interrupting my plans right now?
9:3.action: Pause today before your routine tasks and ask God to redirect any plan that is not aligned with His will.
9:3.prayer: Lord Jesus, You know the roads I travel. When my direction drifts from Yours, meet me there. Interrupt me gently, open my eyes to Your light, and turn my journey toward Your purposes. Amen.

9:4.devotion: Struck to the ground, Saul hears Jesus ask why he is persecuting Him. Remarkably, the Lord identifies so closely with His suffering people that harming them is harming Him. This verse comforts believers who face opposition and warns anyone who mistreats Christ's followers.
9:4.reflection: Do I recognize how closely Jesus identifies with His people?
9:4.action: Reach out in a concrete way today to someone who is suffering for their faith or facing hardship for following Christ.
9:4.prayer: Jesus, thank You for being so near to Your people that their pain is Yours. Give courage to those who suffer for Your name, and keep me from ever adding to another believer's burden. Amen.

9:5.devotion: Saul asks who is speaking, and Jesus names Himself. The phrase about kicking against the goads suggests Saul had been resisting conviction, like an ox struggling against the farmer's pointed stick. Prolonged resistance to God's prompting only makes the struggle harder on us.
9:5.reflection: What conviction from God have I been pushing against?
9:5.action: Identify one area where you have resisted God's prompting, and take one honest step of obedience in it today.
9:5.prayer: Lord, forgive me for the times I have kicked against Your gentle prodding. Soften my heart, quiet my resistance, and help me trust that Your direction is always better than my defiance. Amen.

9:6.devotion: Saul's immediate question changes everything: Lord, what do You want me to do? Jesus tells him to go into the city, where further instructions await. Obedience often begins with a next step rather than a full roadmap, and God guides those willing to follow one step at a time.
9:6.reflection: Am I willing to obey God's next step without seeing the whole plan?
9:6.action: Take one small step of obedience you already know God has asked of you, even without knowing where it leads.
9:6.prayer: Father, teach me to say with Saul, Lord, what do You want me to do? Give me faith to take the next step You reveal, trusting You with the steps I cannot yet see. Amen.

9:7.devotion: Saul's companions heard the voice but saw no one. They were witnesses to the event yet untouched by its meaning. The same encounter left one man converted and others merely speechless. Being near God's work is not the same as responding to it.
9:7.reflection: Have I been near God's work without truly responding to it?
9:7.action: Move beyond routine faith today by responding personally to one Scripture you read, rather than only hearing it.
9:7.prayer: Lord, keep me from being a bystander to Your work. When You speak, let me not only hear but respond with my whole heart. Draw me from the edge of the encounter into its center. Amen.

9:8.devotion: Saul rises physically blinded and must be led by the hand into Damascus. The proud persecutor becomes dependent on others, humbled in an instant. Sometimes God allows weakness to teach us reliance, and the community of believers becomes the hands that carry us forward.
9:8.reflection: Where is God teaching me to depend on others?
9:8.action: Ask someone for help with something you would normally handle alone, and thank God for the people He places around you.
9:8.prayer: Father, humility is hard for me. Thank You for the people who lead me by the hand in seasons of weakness. Make me willing to receive help, and equally willing to offer it to others. Amen.

9:9.devotion: For three days Saul sits in darkness without food or drink. These were days of solemn waiting, likely of reflection and prayer, between his encounter with Christ and his baptism and calling. God sometimes works deeply in seasons of quiet and uncertainty before sending us out.
9:9.reflection: How do I respond when God asks me to wait in uncertainty?
9:9.action: Set aside ten minutes of quiet stillness today to pray and wait on God without asking for anything.
9:9.prayer: Lord, waiting is uncomfortable, and darkness is unsettling. Meet me in the in-between seasons. Use quiet days to prepare my heart, and teach me to trust You are working even when I cannot see. Amen.

9:10.devotion: In Damascus, an ordinary disciple named Ananias hears the Lord call his name, and he answers, Here I am, Lord. God uses a faithful, available believer to complete what began on the road. Divine plans often unfold through ordinary people willing to say yes.
9:10.reflection: Would I recognize God's voice calling my name, and would I answer?
9:10.action: Begin your morning by saying to God, Here I am, and stay alert for one person He may want you to serve today.
9:10.prayer: Lord, like Ananias, I want to answer, Here I am. Make me available today, attentive to Your voice and willing to be part of Your work in someone else's life, however small the part. Amen.

9:11.devotion: After Saul's encounter with Christ on the Damascus road, he waited blind in a house on Straight Street. God spoke to Ananias, naming Saul's location and noting that he was praying. Even the fiercest opponent of the church, once halted by Jesus, became a man seeking God in prayer.
9:11.reflection: Who might God surprise me by transforming, including people I have written off?
9:11.action: Spend ten quiet minutes in prayer today, and ask God to soften your view of one person you distrust.
9:11.prayer: Lord, You see every heart, even those I fear or avoid. Teach me to pray honestly and to believe that no one is beyond Your reach. Give me Ananias's willingness to listen when You speak. Amen.

9:12.devotion: God revealed to Ananias that Saul had already seen a vision of him coming to restore his sight. Two visions, given to two different men, were about to meet. God was quietly preparing both sides of a reconciliation neither could have imagined.
9:12.reflection: Where might God already be at work on the other side of a situation I'm afraid of?
9:12.action: Before a difficult conversation today, pause and ask God to show you what He may already be doing in the other person's life.
9:12.prayer: Father, You work on both ends of every encounter. Thank You that You prepare hearts before I arrive. Help me trust Your hidden handiwork and step into situations with courage rather than fear. In Jesus' name, Amen.

9:13.devotion: Ananias honestly voiced his fear and objection to God. Saul had persecuted believers in Jerusalem, and Ananias knew it. Scripture here models that we can bring our genuine concerns to God; yet it also shows that His answers sometimes call us past our comfort.
9:13.reflection: What fear or objection am I holding back from honestly telling God?
9:13.action: Write down one honest complaint or fear you have toward God, then bring it to Him aloud in prayer today.
9:13.prayer: Gracious Lord, thank You that Ananias could speak his fears openly to You. I bring You my hesitations honestly, too. When Your answer asks more of me than I expected, give me grace to trust and obey. Amen.

9:14.devotion: Ananias reminded God that Saul carried official authority to arrest believers who called on Jesus' name. The danger was real, not imagined. Following God's call sometimes means walking toward the very person or place we have good reason to avoid.
9:14.reflection: Is there a place of real risk where God may be asking me to go in obedience?
9:14.action: Name one relationship or situation you've avoided out of fear, and take one safe, concrete step toward engagement this week.
9:14.prayer: Lord, You know the real dangers I face, and You do not dismiss them. Give me discernment and courage to obey You even when obedience feels risky. Keep me grounded in Your wisdom and presence. Amen.

9:15.devotion: God's answer reframed everything: Saul was His chosen instrument to carry His name to Gentiles, kings, and Israel. The persecutor would become a messenger. God's purposes can turn an enemy of the gospel into its boldest ambassador.
9:15.reflection: Do I believe God's purposes are bigger than my categories of who can and cannot be used by Him?
9:15.action: Identify someone you've labeled as unreachable, and begin praying for them by name each day this week.
9:15.prayer: Sovereign God, You choose servants in surprising ways and send Your name to every nation and people. Widen my vision beyond my assumptions. Use even the unlikely, and let me welcome whom You have chosen. Amen.

9:16.devotion: God told Ananias that He would show Saul how much he must suffer for Jesus' name. The call to bear Christ's name included hardship. Scripture honors costly faithfulness without glamorizing pain, reminding us that following Jesus may carry real difficulty.
9:16.reflection: Am I willing to follow Jesus even if faithfulness turns out to be costly?
9:16.action: Consider one comfort you cling to, and ask God in prayer whether you're holding your faith with open or clenched hands.
9:16.prayer: Father, I confess I prefer an easy road. Yet Your servants through every age have faced hardship for Your name. Strengthen me to remain faithful in difficulty, and keep me near You whatever the cost. In Jesus' name, Amen.

9:17.devotion: Ananias obeyed, entered the house, laid hands on Saul, and called him 'Brother Saul.' He announced healing of sight and the filling of the Holy Spirit. The word of welcome from a once-feared victim became the doorway into Saul's new life in Christ.
9:17.reflection: Whom might God be asking me to welcome with the word 'brother' or 'sister'?
9:17.action: Reach out warmly today to someone in your church community who is new, isolated, or different from you.
9:17.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You for the gift of belonging in Your family. Help me extend welcome as freely as Ananias did, calling others brother and sister. Fill Your church anew with Your Spirit and unite us in love. Amen.

9:18.devotion: At once something like scales fell from Saul's eyes, his sight returned, and he rose and was baptized. His restoration was immediate and public. Baptism marked the visible beginning of a transformed life that had begun invisibly on the road.
9:18.reflection: What visible step of obedience might mark my own faith today?
9:18.action: If you've never been baptized, ask a pastor about taking that step; if you have, share your testimony with one person this week.
9:18.prayer: God of new beginnings, You open eyes that are blind and turn lives around completely. Thank You for every public step of obedience that tells the world I belong to You. Make my transformed life a testimony. Amen.

9:19.devotion: After his dramatic encounter with Christ on the Damascus road, blind and shaken, Saul is led into the city. There he receives food and physical strength, and then does something deeply human and spiritually wise: he stays with the believers in Damascus for several days, receiving care and friendship from the very people he once came to arrest.
9:19.reflection: Who has God placed in my life to strengthen me during seasons of change and new beginnings?
9:19.action: Reach out today to one fellow believer who encourages you, and thank them for the strength their friendship brings you.
9:19.prayer: Lord, thank You for meeting me where I am and for the people You provide to strengthen me. Help me receive their care humbly, and to be that kind of refreshing presence for someone else today. Amen.

9:20.devotion: The fierce persecutor becomes a bold proclaimer. Without delay, Saul stands in the same synagogues where he intended to drag believers away, and instead announces that Jesus is the Son of God. His transformed life became his first sermon, and his message flowed directly from his personal encounter with the risen Christ.
9:20.reflection: What has Jesus actually changed in my life, and am I willing to say so out loud?
9:20.action: Share with one person today, in simple honest words, what following Jesus has meant in your own experience.
9:20.prayer: Jesus, You turned Saul's life around completely, and You are still changing lives today. Give me courage to speak of You naturally and truthfully, beginning with my own story. Make my words bold and kind. Amen.

9:21.devotion: The listeners are stunned. They knew Saul's reputation as the one who harmed believers in Jerusalem and came to Damascus with arrest warrants. His preaching made no human sense. This verse captures the amazement that greets genuine conversion: the same voice, a completely different message, and a community trying to reconcile the two.
9:21.reflection: Do I truly believe that no person is beyond the reach of God's transforming grace?
9:21.action: Think of someone you have written off spiritually, and pray for them by name today instead of judging them.
9:21.prayer: Father, You amaze us with Your grace. Forgive me for the times I have assumed someone was too far gone for You. Give me Your eyes to see people as candidates for transformation, not as hopeless cases. Amen.

9:22.devotion: Saul grows stronger and stronger, confounding those who argue against him by proving from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ. His boldness does not come from personality alone but from growing conviction rooted in God's Word. The persecutor becomes a patient, persuasive witness whose confidence deepens as he studies and testifies.
9:22.reflection: Am I growing in my understanding of God's Word, or settling for a faith that never deepens?
9:22.action: Spend twenty minutes today studying a passage about Jesus, and write down one insight you can share with someone this week.
9:22.prayer: Lord, strengthen me in You the way You strengthened Saul. Give me a growing hunger for Your Word and the ability to explain my hope gently and clearly. Deepen my roots so my witness grows stronger. Amen.

9:23.devotion: Faithfulness invites opposition. After many days of bold preaching, Saul's former allies plot to kill him. This passage honestly shows that following Christ can carry real cost, even danger. It does not glorify violence; it records how hostile opposition arose against the gospel, and how Paul's ministry from the very beginning involved suffering for the name of Christ.
9:23.reflection: Am I prepared to keep following Jesus even when it costs me comfort, approval, or safety?
9:23.action: Identify one area where sharing your faith feels risky, and prayerfully decide one faithful step you can take there this week.
9:23.prayer: Father, following You is not always easy or safe. Thank You for witnesses like Saul who kept speaking truth under threat. When faithfulness costs me something, give me courage, wisdom, and peace that You are with me. Amen.

9:24.devotion: The plot becomes known to Saul, yet his enemies watch the city gates day and night, hoping to end his life. The danger is real and persistent.
