Peter did not float out in a trance; he walked out dressed and ready. This teaches that divine help often comes alongside our own simple obedience rather than replacing it.
12:8.reflection: What ordinary, practical step of obedience might God be asking me to take alongside my prayers?
12:8.action: Take one practical step today toward a situation you have only prayed about—such as making a call, writing a plan, or seeking help.
12:8.prayer: Lord, thank You that You care about both the miraculous and the mundane in my life. Help me not only to pray but also to obey Your practical leading each day. Make me ready to follow wherever You lead. Amen.

12:9.devotion: Peter followed the angel out of the prison without realizing it was really happening—he assumed he was seeing a vision. Sometimes God's work is so far beyond our expectations that we can barely recognize it as real. The verse captures the wonder of deliverance that exceeds what faith dared to imagine.
12:9.reflection: Have I been so resigned to my circumstances that I might not recognize God's answer when it comes?
12:9.action: Ask God to open your eyes today to His quiet, unexpected work around you, and note down anything you notice by evening.
12:9.prayer: Father, forgive me for the times my expectations have been smaller than Your goodness. Open my eyes to see Your real, present work in my life, and give me a heart that marvels at Your grace. In Jesus' name, Amen.

12:10.devotion: Peter, awakened by an angel, walks past sleeping guards toward freedom. Even the iron gate opens by itself as he follows step by step. Luke shows God removing obstacle after obstacle, and only when Peter is fully free does the angel depart. Deliverance unfolds one obedient step at a time.
12:10.reflection: Which iron gate in your life might God be asking you to approach one faithful step at a time?
12:10.action: Identify one obstacle you have been avoiding, and take the first small, prayerful step toward it today.
12:10.prayer: Lord, when barriers look impossible, help me to keep walking with You. Open doors in Your timing and teach me to trust You at every guarded step along the way. Amen.

12:11.devotion: Peter had been asleep in chains, seemingly calm until now. Standing free in the street, he finally grasps what happened: the Lord really sent His angel and rescued him from Herod's power. His realization reminds us that God's help often becomes clearest only when we look back on it.
12:11.reflection: When have you only recognized God's rescue in hindsight rather than in the moment?
12:11.action: Write down one past situation where you can now see God's help, and thank Him for it today.
12:11.prayer: Father, open my eyes to the deliverances I have missed along the way. Thank You for rescues I did not notice and for Your hand that never left me. Amen.

12:12.devotion: Thinking it over, Peter goes straight to Mary's home, where believers are gathered praying for him. His rescue answers their prayers, though none of them yet know it. Luke quietly connects the praying church with God's powerful intervention, portraying prayer as the ordinary context for extraordinary deliverance.
12:12.reflection: Whose name do you faithfully bring before God when they face trouble?
12:12.action: Spend ten minutes today praying specifically for someone you know who is in a difficult situation.
12:12.prayer: Lord, thank You for hearing the prayers of Your people, even when we pray in weakness and doubt. Make me faithful to intercede for others and expect You to act. Amen.

12:13.devotion: At the gate, a servant girl named Rhoda answers Peter's knock. Luke gives her a name and a small but memorable role in the story. In a narrative filled with kings, prisons, and angels, God's deliverance reaches its joyful climax at an ordinary doorway with an ordinary servant listening.
12:13.reflection: How might God be using your small, everyday tasks as part of His larger story?
12:13.action: Do one humble task today—answering, greeting, helping—attentively, as service offered to God.
12:13.prayer: Father, thank You that no one is too small or ordinary to be part of Your work. Help me serve faithfully in the simple places You have assigned to me. Amen.

12:14.devotion: Overjoyed to recognize Peter's voice, Rhoda runs inside to announce the news—forgetting to open the gate. Her excitement outruns her practicality. Luke paints a tender, humorous picture of joy so overwhelming that it interrupts everything else, even the very task that would complete the reunion.
12:14.reflection: What good news has God given you that still stirs genuine joy when you recall it?
12:14.action: Share one way God has answered prayer with a friend or family member today, expressing real joy.
12:14.prayer: Lord, revive my joy in Your answers. Forgive me for treating Your goodness as routine. Let my heart run with gladness like Rhoda's when I see You at work. Amen.

12:15.devotion: The praying believers refuse to believe Rhoda, insisting she is out of her mind or that it is Peter's angel. The irony is gentle but pointed: they are praying for Peter's release while doubting the report of it. Luke shows that weak faith can still rest in a strong God.
12:15.reflection: When has my praying been more earnest than my expectancy that God would answer?
12:15.action: Review what you have been praying for lately, and ask God to strengthen your expectancy of His answer.
12:15.prayer: Father, You answer prayers even when our faith wavers. Thank You for Your patience with our doubts. Teach me to pray with hope and to believe You hear me. Amen.

12:16.devotion: Peter keeps knocking until the door finally opens, and the astonished believers see him face to face. His persistence completes what Rhoda's excitement interrupted. The scene ends in wonder: the answer to their prayers stands before them, more real and surprising than they had dared to imagine.
12:16.reflection: What might God be asking you to keep doing persistently while the answer is still behind the door?
12:16.action: Choose one faithful, patient task you have set aside, and resume it today without giving up.
12:16.prayer: Lord, thank You that Your answers are worth waiting for. Give me perseverance to keep knocking, and grace to be astonished again by what You can do. Amen.

12:17.devotion: Peter quietly recounts how the Lord brought him out, sends word to James and the brothers, and then departs for another place. He points away from himself to God, serves the church, and moves on without clinging to the spotlight. Freedom, for Peter, immediately becomes testimony and mission.
12:17.reflection: When God blesses or rescues you, do you turn the moment into testimony or keep the attention for yourself?
12:17.action: Tell someone today how God has helped you, clearly crediting Him rather than yourself.
12:17.prayer: Father, keep me humble in every deliverance You give. Let my stories point to You, strengthen Your church, and send me forward into whatever You have next. Amen.

12:18.devotion: Peter has just been delivered from prison by an angel, and morning reveals the chaos left behind. The guards discovered an empty cell, chains intact, doors locked. Luke captures their confusion and alarm. What human power had contained, God's power had opened overnight without anyone noticing.
12:18.reflection: When God works in ways I did not expect, am I quick to recognize His hand or slow like the puzzled soldiers?
12:18.action: Recall one situation where you saw God's help after the fact, and tell someone about it today.
12:18.prayer: Father, You work even while I sleep and fret. Open my eyes to see Your hand in circumstances that confuse me, and give me peace that trusts Your power. In Jesus' name, Amen.

12:19.devotion: Herod could not accept the impossible escape, so the guards bore the consequences of a failure they could not explain. Herod then left Judea for Caesarea. The passage honestly shows the brutality of earthly power, while quietly showing that Herod's grip on the church had failed.
12:19.reflection: Do I ever let pride keep me from admitting that a situation is beyond my control?
12:19.action: When something goes wrong today, pause before assigning blame and consider first what God might be doing.
12:19.prayer: Lord, guard me from pride that blames others when I am helpless. Help me lead with honesty and humility, and protect those who suffer under unjust authority. In Jesus' name, Amen.

12:20.devotion: Tyre and Sidon depended on Herod's territory for food, so despite his anger they sought peace through Blastus, a royal aide. Luke shows the politics of fear and dependence: people using connections to soften an angry ruler. It is a realistic picture of life under unchecked human power.
12:20.reflection: Where in my life am I depending more on human connections and schemes than on God's provision?
12:20.action: Identify one worry about provision today and bring it to God in prayer before you try to fix it alone.
12:20.prayer: Father, You are my true provider, not the favor of the powerful. Calm my anxiety about daily needs, and give wisdom and honesty in how I seek peace with others. In Jesus' name, Amen.

12:21.devotion: On the appointed day, Herod dressed in royal splendor, sat on his throne, and addressed the delegations from Tyre and Sidon. He staged the scene to impress. Luke sets the stage deliberately: a man enjoying the worship of a desperate crowd, moments before his downfall.
12:21.reflection: Do I seek the spotlight for my own glory, or do I point people toward God in what I do?
12:21.action: Do one good task today quietly, without drawing attention to yourself, simply to serve others.
12:21.prayer: Lord, keep me from loving applause more than serving You. Clothe me with humility rather than self-importance, and let my words honor You, not myself. In Jesus' name, Amen.

12:22.devotion: The crowd, seeking favor and food, shouted that Herod's voice was the voice of a god, not a man. Flattery fed his vanity, and he received it. Scripture warns against both giving and accepting praise that belongs to God alone.
12:22.reflection: Whose praise am I chasing, and have I ever flattered someone at the cost of truth?
12:22.action: Speak one honest word of encouragement today instead of empty flattery, and redirect any praise you receive to God.
12:22.prayer: Father, forgive me for the times I have flattered others or soaked in praise myself. Give me a truthful tongue and a humble heart that gladly gives all glory to You. In Jesus' name, Amen.

12:23.devotion: Because Herod accepted worship meant for God alone, judgment came swiftly through the angel of the Lord, and he died. Luke's point is sober and clear: God does not share His glory. Human pride that demands worship invites God's opposition, however powerful it appears.
12:23.reflection: Is there any pride in my life that I have been protecting instead of surrendering to God?
12:23.action: Name one area of pride aloud in prayer today and ask God to begin humbling and reshaping you there.
12:23.prayer: Holy God, You alone deserve glory. Uproot the pride in my heart before it hardens. Teach me to receive success with thanksgiving and to give every honor back to You. In Jesus' name, Amen.

12:24.devotion: After the drama of persecution, deliverance, and Herod's death, Luke gives a quiet summary: the word of God grew and multiplied. Earthly rulers raged and fell, but God's message kept spreading. This verse anchors the whole chapter in God's unstoppable purposes.
12:24.reflection: Do I trust that God's work will continue even when circumstances around me seem chaotic or hostile?
12:24.action: Read or share a portion of Scripture with someone today, joining God's word in its quiet growth.
12:24.prayer: Lord of the harvest, thank You that Your word cannot be imprisoned or stopped. Make me a willing part of its growth, and strengthen Your church wherever it faces pressure. In Jesus' name, Amen.

12:25.devotion: Barnabas and Saul completed their relief ministry in Jerusalem and returned to Antioch, bringing John Mark with them. A chapter filled with danger closes with faithful servants resuming their calling. God's mission moves forward through ordinary obedience after extraordinary events.
12:25.reflection: After a season of turmoil, am I ready to simply return to the work God has given me?
12:25.action: Return faithfully to one responsibility or ministry task today that disruption may have interrupted.
12:25.prayer: Faithful God, help me serve steadily, not only in dramatic moments but in daily obedience. Bless those who labor alongside me, and use my ordinary faithfulness for Your purposes. In Jesus' name, Amen.

13:1.devotion: The church at Antioch was remarkably diverse. Its prophets and teachers included Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen, and Saul. Different backgrounds, races, and social standings gathered around one Lord, worshipping and serving together. This mixed community became the launching point for the gospel's advance to the nations.
13:1.reflection: How does the diversity of my own church community reflect the breadth of God's kingdom?
13:1.action: Reach out today to a fellow believer whose background or life experience differs from yours, and encourage them.
13:1.prayer: Lord, thank You that Your church gathers people from every background into one family. Help me value brothers and sisters different from me, and serve alongside them with humility and joy. Amen.

13:2.devotion: While the believers at Antioch worshiped and fasted, they were not chasing direction—they were simply attending to the Lord. In that posture of devotion, the Holy Spirit spoke clearly, calling Barnabas and Saul to a specific mission. God often makes His will known to hearts already engaged in worship and surrender.
13:2.reflection: When you seek God's direction, is worship and surrender your starting point, or an afterthought?
13:2.action: Set aside thirty minutes today to worship quietly, fast one meal or distraction, and write down any prompting you sense from God.
13:2.prayer: Holy Spirit, tune my heart to hear You as I worship. Speak clearly into my life, and give me courage to obey when You call me to Your work. Amen.

13:3.devotion: Before sending Barnabas and Saul on their mission, the Antioch church fasted, prayed, and laid hands on them. Their sending was not casual; it was rooted in seeking God together. The laying on of hands expressed fellowship, commissioning, and shared commitment to the work ahead.
13:3.reflection: When have I entrusted a big decision to God through deliberate prayer rather than my own plans alone?
13:3.action: Set aside time today to fast from a meal or a distraction and pray specifically for someone serving God far from home.
13:3.prayer: Father, teach me to seek You before acting. Thank You for communities that send workers out with prayer and support. Make me faithful to pray for those You have commissioned. Amen.

13:4.devotion: Barnabas and Saul traveled to Seleucia and sailed to Cyprus, but Luke is clear about who truly sent them: the Holy Spirit. The church prayed and acted, yet the mission belonged to God. Their obedience carried them across seas, trusting the Spirit's leading rather than their own certainty.
13:4.reflection: Am I willing to follow where the Spirit leads, even when the next step takes me out of my comfort?
13:4.action: Identify one step of obedience God has been prompting, and take it today instead of postponing it.
13:4.prayer: Holy Spirit, You sent Your servants out to distant places, and You still lead Your people today. Give me courage to obey Your prompting, trusting You with where You send me. Amen.

13:5.devotion: Arriving at Salamis on Cyprus, Barnabas and Saul began preaching the word of God in the Jewish synagogues, starting with audiences they understood. John Mark accompanied them as an assistant. This journey models mission that begins faithfully in familiar places before stretching toward new horizons.
13:5.reflection: What familiar places in my own life might be a starting point for sharing God's word?
13:5.action: Share something of God's faithfulness today with someone in an ordinary, familiar setting of your week.
13:5.prayer: Lord, thank You that mission starts where I already am. Open my eyes to the people around me who need Your word, and give me a servant's heart like John's. Amen.

13:6.devotion: Crossing the island to Paphos, the missionaries met Bar-Jesus, a sorcerer and false prophet. The narrative contrasts his deception with the true word of God the travelers carried. Scripture describes such opposition honestly, showing that the gospel advances amid competing voices and spiritual confusion.
13:6.reflection: How do I discern between voices that distort truth and the trustworthy word of God?
13:6.action: Spend time today reading Scripture so you can recognize truth clearly when confusing voices surround you.
13:6.prayer: Father, in a world full of competing voices and half-truths, anchor me in Your word. Give me discernment to recognize deception and courage to hold to the truth. Amen.

13:7.devotion: Sergius Paulus, the Roman proconsul of Cyprus, was an intelligent man who wanted to hear the word of God. Though Bar-Jesus stood near him with influence, the ruler's curiosity was stirred by the gospel message. Even powerful, thoughtful people are drawn to God's word when it is proclaimed.
13:7.reflection: Do I assume some people are beyond interest in God, or do I trust His word to stir any heart?
13:7.action: Offer a genuine spiritual conversation today to someone you might normally assume would not be interested.
13:7.prayer: Lord, You draw people of every rank and intellect to Yourself. Keep me from writing anyone off, and give me boldness to share Your word with those who ask honest questions. Amen.

13:8.devotion: Elymas actively opposed the missionaries, trying to turn Sergius Paulus away from the faith. When someone edges toward God, opposition often appears. The passage shows that resistance to the gospel is real, yet it also prepares readers for the Spirit's power to answer such resistance in the verses that follow.
13:8.reflection: When spiritual opposition or discouragement rises, do I quietly retreat, or do I keep trusting God's power to work?
13:8.action: If you face resistance today while doing right, pause and pray before responding rather than giving up or reacting in anger.
13:8.prayer: Father, thank You that opposition does not stop Your purposes. When I face resistance while following You, steadying my heart, help me stand firm in Your strength and not my own. Amen.

13:9.devotion: Here Saul is first called Paul in Acts, and he confronts Elymas filled with the Holy Spirit, fixing his gaze intently on him. Paul's boldness was not personal aggression but Spirit-led response to deliberate opposition against a seeker. The Spirit equips God's servants at the very moment they face conflict.
13:9.reflection: When confronted with opposition to God's work, do I rely on my own forcefulness or on the Spirit's filling?
13:9.action: Before a difficult conversation today, consciously ask the Holy Spirit to fill and guide your words and responses.
13:9.prayer: Holy Spirit, fill me as You filled Paul, so that my words in conflict come from You, not from pride or anger. Grant me clear eyes and a steadfast heart. Amen.

13:10.devotion: On Paul's first missionary journey, a false prophet named Elymas actively opposed the gospel before Sergius Paulus, the Roman proconsul. Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, confronted him directly, naming the deceptive work that was twisting the truth of God's ways and hindering an influential seeker from hearing the faith.
13:10.reflection: Am I ever tempted to distort or obscure God's truth to serve my own interests?
13:10.action: Identify one place today where honesty costs you something, and choose to speak truth plainly and kindly anyway.
13:10.prayer: Lord, guard my mouth from deceit and my heart from compromise. Give me courage like Paul's to name falsehood graciously, and keep me from ever twisting Your straight ways for my own gain. Amen.

13:11.devotion: Paul announced that God's hand would temporarily blind Elymas, and immediately a dark mist fell on him. This judgment on the man opposing the gospel echoed Paul's own experience of blindness, showing that God defends His message. The miracle was momentary, meant to reveal, not merely punish.
13:11.reflection: When God's truth confronts opposition, do I trust His hand to defend His word?
13:11.action: Where you face resistance for your faith today, respond without retaliation, entrusting the outcome to God in a short prayer.
13:11.prayer: Father, Your hand is mighty to defend the gospel. When I feel outnumbered or opposed, help me not to fight in my own strength but to trust You, speaking truth and leaving consequences in Your hands. Amen.

13:12.devotion: Sergius Paulus, the intelligent Roman proconsul, watched the confrontation between the power of God and the deception of Elymas. What convinced him was not only the astonishing miracle but the teaching of the Lord. He believed, becoming a notable convert on Paul's first missionary journey.
13:12.reflection: Is the teaching of the Lord astonishing me, or have I grown dull to its wonder?
13:12.action: Spend ten extra minutes today reading a Gospel passage slowly, asking God to astonish you afresh with His teaching.
13:12.prayer: Lord Jesus, let Your teaching astonish me again. Rescue me from familiarity that breeds indifference, and give me a heart like Sergius Paulus—open, attentive, and quick to believe all that You have said. Amen.

13:13.devotion: Sailing from Paphos, Paul and his companions reached Perga in Pamphylia. There John Mark, who had joined as a helper, left the team and returned to Jerusalem. Scripture does not state his reasons, but the departure later caused tension between Paul and Barnabas, showing that ministry teams face real human struggles.
13:13.reflection: When following Jesus gets hard or uncertain, do I stay the course or quietly turn back?
13:13.action: Name one commitment you have been tempted to abandon, and take one small step today to keep faith with it.
13:13.prayer: Father, You know my seasons of weariness and wavering. When following You feels difficult, steadies my steps and renew my resolve. Give grace, too, for others who stumble, as You restored John Mark. Amen.

13:14.devotion: Paul and Barnabas moved from Perga to Antioch in Pisidia, a significant city in the highlands of Galatia. Following their custom, they went into the synagogue on the Sabbath and sat down, positioning themselves among people who already knew the Scriptures, ready for whatever door God might open.
13:14.reflection: Am I placing myself where God's word is heard, ready to be used if an opportunity arises?
13:14.action: Choose one natural gathering place this week—a meal, workplace, or neighborhood spot—where you can be present and ready to share faith when invited.
13:14.prayer: Lord, like Paul and Barnabas, make me faithful in ordinary places. Open doors for Your word where I live and work, and give me patience to sit and wait for Your timing rather than forcing my own. Amen.

13:15.devotion: After the customary synagogue reading of the Law and the Prophets, the synagogue rulers extended a courtesy to visiting strangers: if the travelers had a word of encouragement, they were welcome to speak. This simple invitation opened the way for Paul's first recorded sermon in Acts, a message that would spread the gospel widely.
13:15.reflection: When an unexpected opportunity to speak for Christ arises, will I be ready to accept it?
13:15.action: Prepare a two-minute summary of what Christ has done for you today, so you are ready to share it if someone asks.
13:15.prayer: Father, thank You for the open invitations You place in ordinary life. Keep me ready with a word of encouragement rooted in Your word, and give me boldness and gentleness when the moment comes to speak. Amen.

13:16.devotion: Paul stood up in the Antioch synagogue and, with a gesture inviting attention, addressed both the people of Israel and the God-fearing Gentiles present. He began his sermon by gathering his listeners, honoring their heritage while including all who sought God—a pattern showing the gospel's reach to everyone within earshot.
13:16.reflection: Do I speak about God in a way that welcomes all who are seeking Him, not only those like me?
13:16.action: Welcome someone today who is different from you—learn their name, listen well, and treat them as a person God cares about.
13:16.prayer: Lord, widen my vision to include everyone You are calling—people of every background who fear You. Help me to speak of Your grace with warmth that draws hearers in rather than words that exclude. Amen.

13:17.devotion: Paul opened his sermon with Israel's history: God chose the fathers, exalted His people during their years as foreigners in Egypt, and with an uplifted arm—His mighty power—brought them out. Before announcing Jesus, Paul reminded his hearers that their story was always a story of God's sovereign, saving initiative.
13:17.reflection: Can I trace God's faithful hand in my own history, even in seasons when I felt like a stranger?
13:17.action: Write a brief timeline of three moments in your life where you can now see God's faithful hand at work.
13:17.prayer: God of my fathers, You chose Your people long before they could choose You, and Your mighty arm delivered them. Teach me to read my own story the same way—marked by Your faithfulness from beginning to end. Amen.

13:18.devotion: In Paul's synagogue sermon at Pisidian Antioch, he recalls Israel's wilderness years. God patiently bore with a stubborn, murmuring people for about forty years, providing for them despite their rebellion. His endurance reveals a patience far greater than our failures.
13:18.reflection: Where have I experienced God's patience with me, even when my heart wandered?
13:18.action: Thank God today for one specific season when He patiently carried you through difficulty or disobedience.
13:18.prayer: Patient Father, thank You for bearing with me through my wandering seasons. Your patience amazes me. Help me extend that same gracious patience to the people around me today. In Jesus' name, Amen.

13:19.devotion: Paul continues Israel's story: after the wilderness years, God defeated the seven nations of Canaan and distributed the promised land to His people by allotment. What He promised to Abraham, He delivered—showing that God finishes what He begins.
13:19.reflection: What promise of God do I struggle to believe He will actually complete?
13:19.action: Write down one promise from Scripture you need to trust, and pray over it before bed tonight.
13:19.prayer: Faithful God, You kept Your word to Israel across generations. Teach me to trust Your timing when promises seem delayed. Strengthen my faith to rest in Your unfailing commitment to Your word. Amen.

13:20.devotion: Paul summarizes roughly four hundred fifty years under judges—leaders God raised season after season to deliver and guide Israel. Even when the people drifted, God kept providing rescue and leadership, until Samuel the prophet marked a new era.
13:20.reflection: When have I seen God provide guidance or rescue right when I needed it most?
13:20.action: Reach out today to someone who has spiritually guided you, and thank them specifically for their influence.
13:20.prayer: Lord, thank You for the judges, prophets, and mentors You raise up to guide Your people. Thank You for the voices You have placed in my life. Make me willing to guide others toward You. Amen.

13:21.devotion: Israel demanded a king like the nations around them, and God gave them Saul of Benjamin, who ruled forty years. Paul notes this honestly: the request reflected the people's desires, yet God still worked within it according to His larger plan.
13:21.reflection: When have I asked God for something for the wrong reasons, wanting to resemble the world around me?
13:21.action: Examine one current desire today and ask honestly whether it comes from faith or from wanting to fit in.
13:21.prayer: Father, forgive me for the times I have wanted what the world wants rather than what You want. Purify my desires. Teach me to ask according to Your wisdom and Your good purposes. Amen.

13:22.devotion: After removing Saul, God raised up David, giving this remarkable testimony: David was a man after God's own heart, who would do all His will. Not a flawless man—David sinned greatly—but one oriented toward God and willing to obey.
13:22.reflection: Is there an area of my life where I know God's will but have been resisting doing it?
13:22.action: Identify one known act of obedience you have delayed, and take the first concrete step toward it today.
13:22.prayer: God, You saw David's heart and called him Yours. I want that testimony for my life. Give me a heart that delights in You and hands that carry out Your will, even when it costs me. Amen.

13:23.devotion: Paul reaches his sermon's turning point: from David's line, according to God's promise, God brought Israel a Savior—Jesus. Centuries of history converge on one person. The whole story of Israel exists to carry the promise of redemption to the world.
13:23.reflection: How does seeing Jesus as the climax of God's long story change the way I read Scripture?
13:23.action: Read one Old Testament passage today and look for how it points forward to Christ.
13:23.prayer: Father, thank You that all of history bends toward Jesus, the promised Savior. Open my eyes to see Him across every page of Scripture, and deepen my gratitude for Your plan of rescue. Amen.

13:24.devotion: Before Jesus appeared publicly, John the Baptist prepared the way, preaching a baptism of repentance to all Israel. Hearts had to be made ready. Repentance was the doorway through which people would recognize and receive their Savior.
13:24.reflection: Is there anything in my heart that needs repentance before I can fully welcome Jesus' work in my life?
13:24.action: Spend ten quiet minutes today asking God to reveal anything you need to confess, then confess it to Him.
13:24.prayer: Lord, thank You for those who prepare hearts, and for repentance that makes room for You. Search me now. Turn me from whatever hinders me, and make my heart ready to receive Christ afresh. Amen.

13:25.devotion: As John finished his course, he deflected any attention from himself: he was not the Christ, and he was unworthy to untie the Coming One's sandals. John knew his role, embraced its limits, and pointed everything toward Jesus.
13:25.reflection: In what areas of my life do I seek attention for myself rather than pointing others to Jesus?
13:25.action: Do one good deed today quietly, without mentioning it to anyone, simply to serve others in Christ's name.
13:25.prayer: Lord Jesus, John knew he was unworthy even to carry Your sandals. Humble my heart. Free me from needing recognition, and make my life a clear signpost pointing others toward You. Amen.

13:26.devotion: In Pisidian Antioch, Paul addresses synagogue worshippers, both Jews and God-fearing Gentiles. He tells them plainly that the message of salvation has come to them personally. The gospel is not distant news but an invitation addressed directly to everyone listening, across every background and lineage.
13:26.reflection: Do I hear the gospel as a message sent personally to me, not just to others?
13:26.action: Share with one person today how the message of salvation has come to you personally.
13:26.prayer: Lord, thank You that Your word of salvation has been sent to me. Help me receive it fresh today and carry it gladly to others, so no one near me misses this gracious invitation. Amen.

13:27.devotion: Paul observes that the people and rulers of Jerusalem condemned Jesus even while the prophets were read aloud each Sabbath. They had the Scriptures in their hands yet failed to recognize the One the prophets foretold. Familiarity with holy words is no guarantee of knowing the One they point to.
13:27.reflection: Could I be reading the Bible regularly while missing the Savior it reveals?
13:27.action: Before reading Scripture today, pause and ask God to help you see Jesus in the passage.
13:27.prayer: Father, keep me from hearing Your word without knowing Your Son. Open my ears to the voices of the prophets and my eyes to Jesus on every page, so familiarity never becomes blindness. Amen.

13:28.devotion: Paul recounts the injustice of Jesus' trial: though no grounds for death were found in Him, He was still condemned. Paul names this wrong honestly, showing that Jesus suffered as an innocent man. The gospel rests on One who died without guilt of His own.
13:28.reflection: How does the innocence of Jesus deepen my gratitude for what He endured for me?
13:28.action: Thank God in writing today that Jesus stood in your place though He had no fault of His own.
13:28.prayer: Lord Jesus, You were condemned without cause so that I, who have cause, could be declared righteous. Thank You for bearing unjust suffering for my sake. Teach me to live in grateful response. Amen.

13:29.devotion: Paul notes that everything written about Jesus was fulfilled, even His burial. After the crucifixion, Jesus' body was taken down and laid in a tomb. The sorrow of that grave is part of the story, a real ending that sets the stage for what God was about to do.
13:29.reflection: Do I trust that even the darkest chapters of the gospel story were held within God's purposes?
13:29.action: Bring one sorrow or buried hope to God in prayer today, entrusting it to His larger story.
13:29.prayer: Father, even the tomb fell within Your written plan. When my story enters dark and quiet places, help me remember that endings are not final with You, and that Your purposes reach beyond what I can see. Amen.

13:30.devotion: After the stark account of condemnation and burial, Paul turns with one of Scripture's great turning points: God raised Jesus from the dead. Human rejection and death did not have the last word. The resurrection is God's decisive answer, the heart of the message Paul preached.
13:30.reflection: How would my outlook today change if I truly lived in the light of the resurrection?
13:30.action: Recite the phrase 'God raised Him from the dead' in prayer whenever discouragement strikes you today.
13:30.prayer: Father, thank You that death was not the end. Your Son lives, and Your power has already acted. Fill my day with resurrection hope, especially in the places where I feel defeated. Amen.

13:31.devotion: Paul grounds the resurrection in witnesses: for many days, people who had followed Jesus from Galilee saw Him alive. The claim was not hidden or private; it was testified by those who knew Him. Christian faith rests on the testimony of those who encountered the risen Christ.
13:31.reflection: Whose testimony first brought the reality of Jesus to life for me?
13:31.action: Contact someone today to thank them for the witness they have given you about Christ.
13:31.prayer: Lord, thank You for the witnesses who saw You alive and passed the news down to me. Make me a faithful witness in my own circle, sharing what I have received with clarity and love. Amen.

13:32.devotion: Paul calls his message glad tidings, the good news of a promise made long ago to Israel's fathers now coming true. The resurrection is not an isolated event but the fulfillment of an ancient promise. What God pledged to previous generations, He has accomplished.
13:32.reflection: Where do I need reminding that God keeps promises across long stretches of time?
13:32.action: Write down one promise from Scripture you are still waiting on God to fulfill, and pray over it.
13:32.prayer: Faithful God, You made promises to the fathers and fulfilled them in Your Son. Teach me to wait on Your timing without despairing, trusting that Your word does not return empty across the generations. Amen.

13:33.devotion: Paul declares that God has fulfilled the promise for the children of the fathers by raising up Jesus, and he cites the second Psalm: 'You are My Son.' The resurrection publicly confirms Jesus as the Son of God, the promised King. Paul's preaching joins Scripture and event together as one glad message.
13:33.reflection: How does the Father's declaration over Jesus shape the way I view His authority in my life?
13:33.action: Read the second Psalm today and note one way it enlarges your picture of who Jesus is.
13:33.prayer: Father, thank You for raising Jesus and declaring Him Your Son. I bow before Him as the promised King. Reign in my decisions, my relationships, and my heart today, that His lordship would be evident in me. Amen.

13:34.devotion: In Paul's sermon at Pisidian Antioch, he proclaims that Jesus' resurrection fulfills God's promise to David. Because Christ was raised never to die again, God's covenant mercies are now certain and available. The resurrection is not merely an event but the guarantee of God's steadfast faithfulness to His people.
13:34.reflection: Where in my life do I need to trust that God's promises are as sure as the empty tomb?
13:34.action: Write down one promise of God you are clinging to today, and thank Him aloud that Christ's resurrection secures it.
13:34.prayer: Risen Lord, thank You that Your resurrection makes God's mercies certain. Help me rest today in promises that cannot fail, and live with the hope that death itself has been defeated. Amen.

13:35.devotion: Paul quotes another psalm to show that Scripture anticipated the Messiah's victory over decay. While every human body undergoes corruption after death, God's Holy One would not. Paul uses the psalmist's words to argue that Jesus, the Holy One, is uniquely raised incorruptible by the Father.
13:35.reflection: How does knowing that Jesus' body did not decay deepen my confidence in His identity and power?
13:35.action: Read one psalm today slowly, looking for hints of the Messiah, and note what you discover.
13:35.prayer: Father, Your Word testified beforehand that Your Holy One would rise. Thank You that Scripture points faithfully to Jesus. Give me eyes to see Him throughout the whole Bible and heart to trust Him fully. Amen.

13:36.devotion: Paul contrasts David with Jesus. David faithfully served God's purposes in his own generation, then died and was buried, seeing decay like all people. This honors David's faithful service while showing he was not the promised one. Even the great king points beyond himself to a greater Son to come.
13:36.reflection: Am I serving God's purposes in my own generation, with the people and needs right in front of me?
13:36.action: Identify one person in your daily circle who needs help, and serve them practically before the day ends.
13:36.prayer: Lord, like David, help me serve Your purposes in my own generation faithfully and humbly. Teach me to invest my days in the people You have placed near me, trusting You with the results. Amen.

13:37.devotion: Paul's sermon reaches its climax: the One whom God raised, Jesus, saw no decay. Unlike David, and unlike every human king or hero, Jesus conquered death completely. This distinction is the heart of the gospel—God has vindicated His Son, and through Him offers resurrection life to all who believe.
13:37.reflection: Is my hope anchored in a person who conquered death, or in things that decay?
13:37.action: Share with one person today, in simple words, why Jesus' resurrection matters to your hope.
13:37.prayer: Jesus, unlike every other, You rose and saw no corruption. Anchor my hope in You alone, the Living One. When I face loss and mortality, lift my eyes to Your victory and promised life. Amen.

13:38.devotion: In Paul's sermon at Pisidian Antioch, he announces the heart of the gospel: forgiveness of sins comes through Jesus. After tracing Israel's story to David's greater Son, Paul declares that the pardon the law pointed toward is now freely preached to all who will receive it through this Man.
13:38.reflection: Where have I been looking for forgiveness apart from Jesus?
13:38.action: Write down one sin you've been carrying, and thank Jesus aloud for forgiving it today.
13:38.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You that forgiveness is found in You alone. Help me stop striving to earn what You freely give, and let me rest today in Your complete pardon. Amen.

13:39.devotion: Paul continues: everyone who believes is justified from all things the law of Moses could never justify. This was radical good news. Rules and rituals, however sacred, could not make anyone right with God. Faith in Christ accomplishes what human effort never could, for all people alike.
13:39.reflection: Am I secretly trying to justify myself by performance instead of trusting Christ alone?
13:39.action: Identify one way you measure your worth by achievement, and consciously hand that burden to Christ in prayer.
13:39.prayer: Father, thank You that I am justified by believing in Jesus, not by my record. Free me from the exhausting treadmill of earning Your acceptance, and anchor my identity in Your grace. Amen.

13:40.devotion: Paul then offers a sober warning: beware, or the prophets' words may come upon you. Good news carries responsibility. To hear the gospel and dismiss it is dangerous. Paul urges his hearers to take the message seriously rather than shrug off the gracious opportunity set before them.
13:40.reflection: Is there a warning from God's Word I've been politely ignoring?
13:40.action: Name one area where you've resisted God's prompting, and take one small obedient step toward it today.
13:40.prayer: Gracious God, give me a soft heart that takes Your Word seriously. Keep me from complacency, and help me respond to Your warnings with humility instead of stubbornness. Amen.

13:41.devotion: Paul quotes the prophet Habakkuk, who warned that God's astonishing work could be met with unbelief. Paul applies it to his audience: God is acting in their very days through Jesus, yet some will refuse to believe even when it's declared to them. Wonder can harden into scorn if ignored.
13:41.reflection: Could God be doing something wonderful right in front of me that I've dismissed as unbelievable?
13:41.action: Pause midday and ask God to open your eyes to His work around you, then note one thing you notice.
13:41.prayer: Lord, don't let me miss what You are doing in my days. Guard me from scorn and unbelief, and give me eyes of faith to recognize and welcome Your work. Amen.

13:42.devotion: After Paul finished preaching in the Pisidian Antioch synagogue, the response was immediate hunger. The Gentiles who heard begged that these words be preached to them again the next Sabbath. The gospel had stirred something in them they could not let go of for a whole week. When God's word takes root, it creates longing for more.
13:42.reflection: When did God's word last leave you hungry to hear more?
13:42.action: Set aside fifteen extra minutes today to reread a passage that stirred you recently and sit with it quietly.
13:42.prayer: Lord, give me that holy hunger of the Gentiles who begged to hear more of Your word. Keep my heart soft and curious, never indifferent to Your truth. Feed me daily, I ask in Jesus' name, amen.

13:43.devotion: When the synagogue service ended, many Jews and devout proselytes did not simply go home. They followed Paul and Barnabas, wanting more conversation. The missionaries urged them to continue in the grace of God, teaching that the Christian life begins by grace and continues by grace, not by human effort or religious performance.
13:43.reflection: Are you trying to continue in your own strength instead of God's grace?
13:43.action: Write one area where you have been striving in your own effort, and consciously entrust it to God's grace today.
13:43.prayer: Father, thank You that Your grace is not only the door into faith but the path of every day after. Help me continue in grace, not in weary self-effort. Teach me to receive what I cannot earn, in Jesus' name, amen.

13:44.devotion: Word about Paul and Barnabas spread through the city during the week. By the next Sabbath, almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of God. This verse shows how God's message travels through ordinary conversations and excited testimony. No advertising campaign brought that crowd; simply people telling people what they had heard.
13:44.reflection: Whom have you told this week about what God has done or taught you?
13:44.action: Share one thing you learned or received from God with a friend or family member in a natural conversation today.
13:44.prayer: Lord, You turned one synagogue sermon into a whole city gathering. Use my ordinary conversations the same way. Give me courage to mention You naturally, and let Your word draw people to hear, in Jesus' name, amen.

13:45.devotion: When the synagogue leaders saw the huge crowds, envy filled them. They began contradicting and opposing what Paul taught. The text honestly shows that opposition to the gospel is sometimes rooted not in careful disagreement but in jealousy over attention and influence. Envy distorts judgment and turns religious people against God's own message.
13:45.reflection: Can you name any envy in your heart toward how God is working in someone else's life?
13:45.action: If you feel jealous of someone's success or ministry today, pray a sincere blessing over that person by name.
13:45.prayer: Father, search my heart and expose envy before it hardens into opposition. Forgive me for the times I resented Your blessing on others. Teach me to celebrate every place Your word flourishes, even when I am not at the center, amen.

13:46.devotion: Facing opposition, Paul and Barnabas grew bold rather than timid. They declared that the word had rightly come to the Jews first, but since those listeners rejected it, they would turn to the Gentiles. Luke presents rejection as a serious self-judgment, while the missionaries responded not with despair but with renewed obedience to their wider calling.
13:46.reflection: How do you respond when your testimony is rejected: with silence and discouragement, or with boldness?
13:46.action: If you have grown timid about your faith after a rebuff, take one simple step of openness again today.
13:46.prayer: Lord Jesus, when I face rejection for Your name, replace my discouragement with boldness. Remind me that rejection is not the end of the story, and that Your word is meant for every person and every nation, amen.

13:47.devotion: Paul and Barnabas anchored their mission in Scripture, quoting the Lord's word about being set as a light to the Gentiles, for salvation to the ends of the earth. Their turning to the Gentiles was not a tantrum but obedience to God's ancient purpose. God's plan had always stretched beyond one people to every nation.
13:47.reflection: Do you see yourself as part of God's light reaching people far from Him?
13:47.action: Pray by name today for one person or people group far from God, and consider one way you can be light to them.
13:47.prayer: Father, You set Your servants as a light to the ends of the earth, and in Christ You include me in that mission. Make my life genuinely luminous in my home, workplace, and neighborhood, that others might find salvation in You, amen.

13:48.devotion: When the Gentiles heard that God's salvation was for them too, they were glad and glorified the word of the Lord, and many believed. Luke describes their believing as those appointed to eternal life, emphasizing God's gracious initiative. Their joy reminds us that receiving the gospel is not a burden but glad news worth celebrating.
13:48.reflection: Does the gospel still make you glad, or has familiarity dulled your joy?
13:48.action: Thank God today, out loud or in writing, for three specific gifts of His grace in your life.
13:48.prayer: Lord, restore my gladness in Your word. Forgive me for treating the gospel as ordinary. Like the Gentiles of old, let me hear it again as news meant for me, and respond with joy, praise, and belief, in Jesus' name, amen.

13:49.devotion: The passage closes with quiet momentum: the word of the Lord was being spread throughout all the region. Despite envy and opposition, God's message kept moving from town to town. This reminds us that the gospel's advance does not finally depend on favorable circumstances but on God's power accompanying His word through faithful people.
13:49.reflection: Where in your own region, your circles and community, might God want His word to spread through you?
13:49.action: Identify one person in your wider circle who may never have heard the gospel clearly, and pray for a chance to share it this week.
13:49.prayer: Father, Your word spread through a whole region because ordinary believers carried it. Send Your word through my region too, and make me a willing carrier. Overturn every obstacle with Your power, and let many come to believe, in Jesus' name, amen.

13:50.devotion: In Pisidian Antioch, Paul and Barnabas had preached the gospel widely, but opposition arose. Influential residents were persuaded to reject the message, and the missionaries faced persecution and were forced out of the region. Even faithful witness can meet resistance from people in positions of influence.
13:50.reflection: When my faith or witness is rejected, do I assume something has gone wrong, or remember that opposition accompanied the gospel from the start?
13:50.action: If you faced rejection for your faith recently, write down one sentence entrusting that situation to God rather than replaying it today.
13:50.prayer: Lord Jesus, when opposition comes because I follow You, steady my heart. Keep me from bitterness toward those who reject the message, and help me remain faithful in Your strength. Amen.

13:51.devotion: Expelled from Antioch, Paul and Barnabas shook the dust from their feet, an action Jesus had described for those whose message was not received. It was a symbolic testimony, not an act of revenge. Then they moved on, continuing the mission rather than dwelling on the rejection.
13:51.reflection: Is there a rejection or disappointment I keep carrying when God may be calling me to release it and move forward?
13:51.action: Name one discouragement you have been dwelling on, and deliberately take one small step toward your next God-given task today.
13:51.prayer: Father, You know the doors that have closed before me. Help me release what I cannot control, trust You with the outcome, and walk obediently into whatever You place next. Amen.

13:52.devotion: Though the missionaries were driven out, the new believers in Antioch were not defeated. Scripture says they were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit. Their joy did not depend on comfortable circumstances but on the presence of God and the word of grace they had received.
13:52.reflection: Does my joy rest on easy circumstances, or on the Holy Spirit's presence with me in difficult ones?
13:52.action: Thank God in prayer for three specific gifts of His grace in your life, especially any that came through hard seasons.
13:52.prayer: Holy Spirit, fill me anew with the joy that circumstances cannot take away. Remind me that Your presence is my deepest treasure, and let that joy show in how I live today. Amen.

14:1.devotion: Undeterred by persecution, Paul and Barnabas continued their practice of beginning in the synagogue in Iconium. As they spoke, God worked through their words, and many Jews and Greeks believed. Perseverance in witness, coupled with God's work in hearts, bore fruit even after recent rejection.
14:1.reflection: Am I willing to keep sharing my faith consistently, or does one discouraging response make me stop speaking of Christ?
14:1.action: Share one simple sentence about God's goodness with a coworker, neighbor, or friend today, however brief.
14:1.prayer: Lord, give me courage to keep speaking of You even when results seem slow or responses are mixed. Work in hearts I cannot see, and use my ordinary words for Your purposes. Amen.

14:2.devotion: Not everyone in Iconium welcomed the message. Some who disbelieved worked to turn the Gentile population against the believers, spreading influence that poisoned minds toward them. The gospel's arrival often exposed existing divisions, and the missionaries faced opposition that was social and relational as well as verbal.
14:2.reflection: When I hear negative talk about another believer or church, do I check it carefully, or let someone else's attitude shape my mind?
14:2.action: Refuse to pass along one piece of gossip or criticism about a person or church today; choose silence or a kind word instead.
14:2.prayer: Father, guard my mind from being poisoned against others by hearsay. Make me slow to judge, quick to love, and discerning about the voices I let influence me. Amen.

14:3.devotion: The missionaries faced real opposition, yet instead of moving on quickly, they stayed and kept speaking boldly. Their courage came from the Lord, who backed their message about His grace with signs and wonders. This passage shows a partnership: God's servants open their mouths, and God confirms the truth they proclaim. Bold witness and divine affirmation belong together, so the gospel of grace advances even amid resistance.
14:3.reflection: Where is God asking you to speak about His grace, even when it feels risky?
14:3.action: Name one person who needs to hear about God's grace, and share a sentence of your testimony with them today.
14:3.prayer: Lord, thank You that Your grace speaks through Your people. Give me courage to share Your word plainly, and work through my witness in ways only You can, confirming Your truth as I obey. Amen.

14:4.devotion: The city of Iconium split over the apostles' message: some aligned with the Jewish leaders who opposed the gospel, others sided with the apostles. The gospel does not leave people neutral; it calls for a response. Even division, painful as it is, reveals that the message matters deeply.
14:4.reflection: When following Christ puts me at odds with people around me, do I stand with Him or quietly blend in?
14:4.action: Identify one area where pressure from others tempts you to compromise your faith, and decide now how you will respond.
14:4.prayer: Lord Jesus, You divide hearts by Your truth. When loyalty to You sets me apart from others, give me grace to stand firm without pride, and to love those who choose differently. Amen.

14:5.devotion: Opposition in Iconium escalated from words to a plot of violence, as Gentiles, Jews, and city rulers attempted to mistreat and stone the missionaries. The danger was real and coordinated. This narrative describes ancient events; it records, rather than endorses, the hostility believers sometimes faced for their witness.
14:5.reflection: How would I respond if my faithfulness to Christ carried real social or personal cost?
14:5.action: Pray by name today for one believer or community facing hostility for their faith, asking God to strengthen and protect them.
14:5.prayer: Father, You see Your people who face hostility for following You. Strengthen and protect them, sustain their courage, and teach me to pray faithfully for those who suffer for Christ's name. Amen.

14:6.devotion: Aware of the plot against them, Paul and Barnabas fled to Lystra and Derbe and the surrounding region. Escaping danger was not cowardice; it was wise stewardship of their lives and mission. They did not abandon the work but carried it to new places where the gospel could be preached.
14:6.reflection: Do I confuse faithfulness with unnecessary risk, and miss God's wisdom in knowing when to stay and when to step away?
14:6.action: Consider one situation where wisdom calls you to step back or seek safety, and take one practical step toward that today.
14:6.prayer: Lord, give me wisdom to discern when to stand firm and when You are redirecting my steps. Protect me from needless danger, and use every turn of my path for Your glory. Amen.

14:7.devotion: Paul and Barnabas had just fled danger in Iconium, yet they did not retreat into silence. Arriving in Lystra, they continued their central task: preaching the good news of Jesus. Their hardships did not cancel their calling. Wherever they went, whatever they faced, they kept speaking about Christ.
14:7.reflection: What difficulty in my life has tempted me to go quiet about my faith?
14:7.action: Share one simple word about God's goodness with someone today, even if circumstances feel discouraging.
14:7.prayer: Lord Jesus, like Paul and Barnabas, help me keep proclaiming Your gospel even when the road is hard. Give me courage to speak of You wherever You send me. Amen.

14:8.devotion: In Lystra sat a man who had never walked, disabled from birth. In that ancient setting he had no means of healing and likely depended on others daily. Luke's careful description sets the stage for what God was about to do through Paul, drawing attention to the man's long need.
14:8.reflection: Do I believe God sees needs in my life that have gone unmet for years?
14:8.action: Notice someone today who lives with limitation or need, and offer them a kind word or practical help.
14:8.prayer: Father, You see every person the world overlooks, including me in my weaknesses. Thank You that no need of mine is hidden from Your sight. Help me see others as You do. Amen.

14:9.devotion: As the man listened to Paul preach, faith rose in his heart. Paul, watching him closely, perceived that God had given this man faith to be healed. The gospel itself became the channel of the man's trust. Faith came as he heard, and Paul was attentive enough to notice it.
14:9.reflection: When I hear God's word, do I listen with a heart open to faith, or merely with curiosity?
14:9.action: Spend ten minutes today listening to or reading God's word slowly, asking Him to stir genuine faith in you.
14:9.prayer: Lord, let Your word awaken real faith in me, not just interest. Open my heart as this man opened his. Make me attentive to what You are doing in others too. Amen.

14:10.devotion: Paul called out boldly for the man to stand, and the man leaped up and walked. What had never happened in his life happened in a moment. This healing pointed beyond itself to the power of the risen Christ at work through His servants, confirming the message Paul preached.
14:10.reflection: Where in my life am I being invited to rise and walk in strength God provides?
14:10.action: Take one step today toward something God has been calling you to do but fear or weakness has kept you from.
14:10.prayer: God of power, You can strengthen what has been weak my whole life. Help me rise when You call and walk in the new life You give. I trust You. Amen.

14:11.devotion: The crowds of Lystra, seeing the miracle, reacted according to their pagan background: they declared the gods had come as men. They recognized supernatural power but completely misread its source. Not every awe-inspired response to God's work is true worship, and miracles alone did not produce the gospel in their hearts.
14:11.reflection: Have I ever been impressed by something impressive, without actually responding to God Himself?
14:11.action: Examine your heart today: name one thing you admire or pursue, and ask whether it draws you closer to God or replaces Him.
14:11.prayer: Lord, guard me from being amazed by gifts while missing the Giver. Keep my worship anchored in You alone, not in experiences or wonders. Reveal any misplaced awe in my heart. Amen.

14:12.devotion: The people assigned local identities to the visitors: Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul, Hermes, since he did the speaking. This shows how easily culture frames what it cannot understand. Paul and Barnabas were mistaken for the very idols they came to renounce, an irony underscoring the need for clear testimony.
14:12.reflection: When people observe my life, whom do they think I am pointing to?
14:12.action: In one conversation today, speak of Jesus by name so the credit for your hope lands where it belongs.
14:12.prayer: Father, let my life point clearly to Jesus, not to myself. Forgive me when my words or silence blur the testimony. Make me a clear signpost to Your Son. Amen.

14:13.devotion: The priest of Zeus, whose temple stood before the city, arrived with oxen and garlands, preparing to offer sacrifices to Paul and Barnabas. Honor was coming swiftly and sincerely, yet it was entirely misdirected. Public acclaim for God's servants can arrive dressed as devotion, and it comes with real pressure.
14:13.reflection: How do I respond when praise comes my way for something God has done?
14:13.action: When someone compliments you today, briefly and sincerely redirect the credit to God in your reply.
14:13.prayer: Lord, when applause comes, keep me humble and quick to redirect it to You. Protect me from enjoying honor that belongs to You alone. Guard my heart in moments of praise. Amen.

14:14.devotion: Hearing what was happening, Barnabas and Paul tore their clothes, an ancient sign of grief and alarm, and rushed into the crowd crying out. They refused worship violently and immediately. Their example teaches that God's servants must deflect glory decisively, even at the cost of popularity in the moment.
14:14.reflection: Is there any praise I have quietly allowed that belongs to God alone?
14:14.action: Identify one area where you have accepted credit for God's work, and correct it today in word or writing.
14:14.prayer: Father, give me the urgency of Paul and Barnabas to guard Your glory. Tear away any pride in me that enjoys misplaced worship. Let all honor return to You, now and always. Amen.

14:15.devotion: When the crowds in Lystra tried to worship Paul and Barnabas after a healing, the missionaries tore their clothes in distress and insisted they were only ordinary humans. They redirected all honor to the living God, the Creator of heaven, earth, and sea, urging the people to abandon worthless idols and turn to Him alone.
14:15.reflection: In what areas of my life am I tempted to give glory or trust to created things rather than to the living Creator?
14:15.action: Identify one thing you tend to rely on or admire more than God today, and deliberately redirect that trust or praise to Him in prayer.
14:15.prayer: Living God, Maker of heaven and earth, forgive me for the small idols I cling to. Turn my heart from every useless thing, and let all my worship and trust rest in You alone today. Amen.

14:16.devotion: Continuing his words at Lystra, Paul acknowledged that in past generations God had allowed the nations to go their own ways. This was not approval of idolatry, but a recognition of God's patient forbearance across history, setting the stage for the good news that now called all people to turn to Him.
14:16.reflection: Where might I mistake God's patience with my own wandering as permission to keep going my own way?
14:16.action: Name one habit or attitude you have excused as harmless, and honestly bring it before God today, asking Him to redirect your steps.
14:16.prayer: Patient Father, thank You for bearing with wandering hearts, including mine. Do not let me mistake Your forbearance for indifference. Gently call me back from my own ways and set my feet on Your path. Amen.

14:17.devotion: Paul told the Lystrans that even though God once let nations walk their own ways, He never left Himself without a witness. The rain, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness people enjoyed were constant testimonies to God's kindness, evidence of a generous Provider reaching toward them even before they knew His name.
14:17.reflection: When did I last notice God's everyday kindnesses, like food, weather, and moments of joy, as witnesses to His care?
14:17.action: Take five minutes outdoors or by a window today and thank God specifically for three ordinary gifts of provision you usually overlook.
14:17.prayer: Generous Provider, Your kindness surrounds me in rain, harvest, bread, and gladness, yet I rarely pause to see it. Open my eyes to Your daily witness in the world and awaken gratitude in my heart. Amen.

14:18.devotion: Paul's humble words barely stopped the Lystran crowds from offering sacrifices to him and Barnabas. The people were so swept up in excitement and misplaced enthusiasm that even a clear, urgent correction struggled to turn them. The scene shows how easily crowds can fix their devotion on the wrong object.
14:18.reflection: How quickly does my enthusiasm attach itself to people or experiences rather than to God Himself?
14:18.action: If you admire a teacher, leader, or public figure today, pause and thank God for the gift while deliberately reserving your worship for Him alone.
14:18.prayer: Lord, keep my admiration from becoming misplaced devotion. Guard me from crowd excitement that exalts people above You. Anchor my worship where it belongs, on You, the true and living God. Amen.

14:19.devotion: Opponents from Antioch and Iconium arrived in Lystra and turned the fickle crowd, which had just tried to honor Paul, against him. Paul was stoned and dragged outside the city, left for dead. This verse soberly records real hostility the apostles faced while preaching the gospel; it describes what happened, not what victims deserve.
14:19.reflection: How do I respond when faithfulness to Christ costs me comfort, reputation, or acceptance?
14:19.action: Pray today for a Christian facing persecution for their faith, and ask God for steadfast courage in your own far smaller difficulties.
14:19.prayer: Father, You see Your children around the world who suffer for following Jesus. Strengthen and comfort them. Give me courage to remain faithful when belief is unpopular, and keep me from costly compromise. Amen.

14:20.devotion: After Paul was stoned and dragged out of Lystra, the disciples gathered around him. He rose up, returned into that very city, and the next day continued with Barnabas to Derbe. This passage shows remarkable resilience sustained by God and the caring presence of fellow believers at a desperate moment.
14:20.reflection: Whose presence might God be asking me to provide for someone who has been hurt or knocked down?
14:20.action: Reach out today to someone who has endured a setback or rejection, offering a call, visit, or message of encouragement and practical support.
14:20.prayer: Lord, thank You for friends who gather around us in our worst moments. Make me that kind of companion to others. When I am knocked down, raise me up by Your strength to keep walking with You. Amen.

14:21.devotion: Paul and Barnabas preached the gospel in Derbe and made many disciples, then made a courageous choice: they traveled back through Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, the very places where Paul had been attacked. Rather than avoiding danger, they prioritized strengthening the young churches they had planted there.
14:21.reflection: What difficult place or relationship might I be avoiding that God could be calling me to return to for the sake of others?
14:21.action: Consider one strained relationship or hard place you have avoided, and take one small step toward it today, such as a kind message or prayer for reconciliation.
14:21.prayer: Courageous Savior, You did not avoid hard places for my sake. Give me bravery to return to difficult people and situations when love requires it, and use me to strengthen others in their faith. Amen.

14:22.devotion: On their return journey, Paul and Barnabas strengthened the new disciples, urging them to continue in the faith. They told them plainly that entering the kingdom of God involves passing through many tribulations. This honest teaching prepared believers to endure hardship without surprise, grounding their hope in the kingdom that awaits.
14:22.reflection: When hardships come, do I assume something has gone wrong, or remember that following Jesus often includes trials?
14:22.action: Write down one current hardship, then beside it note one truth about God's kingdom that helps you persevere, and review it when discouragement comes.
14:22.prayer: Faithful God, prepare me for the tribulations Jesus promised, so I am not shaken when they come. Strengthen my soul to continue in the faith, fixing my hope on Your kingdom that outlasts every trouble. Amen.

14:23.devotion: At the close of their missionary journey, Paul and Barnabas strengthened each new congregation by appointing elders to shepherd them. They did not leave these young churches to fend for themselves; they prayed, fasted, and entrusted these leaders to the Lord in whom the believers had trusted.
14:23.reflection: Who am I intentionally praying for and entrusting to God's care today?
14:23.action: Choose one church leader today, pray for them, and send a short note of encouragement and thanks.
14:23.prayer: Lord, thank You for shepherds who watch over Your flock. Strengthen the leaders of my church, guard them in Your truth, and help me support them with prayer and encouragement rather than criticism. In Jesus' name, amen.

14:24.devotion: Paul and Barnabas pressed on through Pisidia into Pamphylia, retracing territory on their return journey. Even the travel verses of Acts remind us that God's work unfolds step by step, through ordinary roads and regions, as faithful messengers carried the gospel onward.
14:24.reflection: Am I willing for God to use me in the ordinary, unglamorous stretches of my daily routine?
14:24.action: During one routine task today, such as a commute or errand, consciously offer that moment to God in a brief prayer.
14:24.prayer: Father, You work through everyday journeys as much as dramatic moments. Teach me to see my ordinary routes and routines as places where You can be present and at work. Keep me faithful on the road today. Amen.

14:25.devotion: On the way home, Paul and Barnabas preached the word in Perga, a city they had passed through earlier, then traveled on to Attalia to find a ship. Their return trip was not a hurried exit; they kept proclaiming the word even while heading back to their sending church.
14:25.reflection: Do I finish my commitments faithfully, or do I slack off once the goal is nearly reached?
14:25.action: Identify one task you have left unfinished and take a concrete step today to complete it faithfully.
14:25.prayer: Lord Jesus, You deserve faithful labor to the very end, not weary shortcuts. Help me finish well what You have placed in my hands today, speaking and living Your word even in the final, unnoticed stretch. Amen.

14:26.devotion: Sailing from Attalia, Paul and Barnabas returned to Antioch, the church that had commended them to the grace of God. Their journey was complete, and they came back to the community whose prayers and sending had sustained the work from the very beginning.
14:26.reflection: Whose prayers and support have carried me, and have I told them so?
14:26.action: Contact one person who has supported you spiritually and thank them specifically today for their part in your life.
14:26.prayer: Gracious God, thank You for the people and churches that send, pray, and stand behind Your work. Help me remember I never serve alone, and give me a grateful heart that honors those You have used to sustain me. Amen.

14:27.devotion: Gathered back in Antioch, Paul and Barnabas called the church together and reported all that God had done with them, especially that He had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles. They credited God, not themselves, and the church rejoiced at His saving work among all peoples.
14:27.reflection: When I share good news about my life, do I tell what God has done or focus on my own efforts?
14:27.action: Share with a friend or family member today one specific way you have seen God at work in your life recently.
14:27.prayer: Father, You opened the door of faith to the Gentiles, showing Your heart for every nation. Give me eyes to recognize Your work around me and a humble tongue that reports Your deeds rather than my own. Amen.

14:28.devotion: After reporting to the church, Paul and Barnabas stayed a long time with the disciples in Antioch. Ministry was not a constant rush; they invested in unhurried fellowship, resting and building relationships with the believers who had been their partners and home base.
14:28.reflection: Do I allow unhurried time with God's people, or does my pace crowd out fellowship and rest?
14:28.action: Schedule relaxed, unhurried time this week with a fellow believer—share a meal, a walk, or a conversation with no agenda.
14:28.prayer: Lord, You made us for fellowship, not ceaseless striving. Thank You for the gift of Christian community and seasons of rest. Teach me to linger with Your people, building friendships that strengthen us all for Your service. Amen.

15:1.devotion: Trouble arose in Antioch when men from Judea insisted that Gentile believers could not be saved unless circumcised according to Moses' custom. This teaching added a human requirement to the gospel of grace, and it stirred the first great doctrinal crisis of the early church.
15:1.reflection: Have I added my own conditions to the gospel of God's grace, for myself or for others?
15:1.action: Write down the gospel in your own words, being careful to state salvation by grace through faith without any added conditions.
15:1.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You that salvation is by grace through faith in You alone. Guard me from every teaching that adds human requirements to Your finished work, and keep my heart humble before Your sufficient gospel. Amen.

15:2.devotion: Paul and Barnabas engaged in sharp dispute with these teachers, refusing to let the gospel be distorted. The church in Antioch then sent Paul and Barnabas and others up to Jerusalem to settle the question with the apostles and elders, seeking resolution together rather than splitting apart.
15:2.reflection: When serious disagreements arise, do I seek godly resolution and wise counsel, or do I simply withdraw and quarrel?
15:2.action: If you are in a current conflict over an important matter, take one step today toward honest, respectful conversation or seeking wise counsel.
15:2.prayer: Father, give me courage to stand for Your truth and humility to seek reconciliation rightly. When disputes arise in Your church, guide us toward wisdom, unity in the gospel, and grace with one another. Through Christ, amen.

15:3.devotion: Paul and Barnabas traveled toward Jerusalem, sent by the church in Antioch to discuss a serious question about Gentile believers. Along the way through Phoenicia and Samaria, they shared how God had brought Gentiles to faith. Their testimony brought great joy to believers everywhere they stopped.
15:3.reflection: When I hear how God has worked in someone else's life, do I respond with joy or with skepticism?
15:3.action: Share one story today of God's work in your life or an answered prayer with a fellow believer, and receive their stories with joy.
15:3.prayer: Father, thank You for every testimony of Your grace. Give me ears that rejoice when I hear of others coming to faith, and a mouth willing to share what You have done in me. Amen.

15:4.devotion: Arriving in Jerusalem, Paul and Barnabas were welcomed by the church, apostles, and elders. They reported everything God had done with them. Even before the coming disagreement, the church received their testimony about God's work among the Gentiles with open hearts and attentive ears.
15:4.reflection: Am I willing to listen fully to what God is doing in others before forming my own judgments?
15:4.action: In your next conversation with a believer from a different background, listen to their whole story before offering any opinion.
15:4.prayer: Lord, make me a welcoming listener. Help me receive the accounts of Your work among all Your people with gladness, giving You credit for everything You have done. Amen.

15:5.devotion: Not everyone welcomed the report. Some believers from a Pharisaic background insisted Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. This was an honest conflict within the early church over what following Christ required, and it set the stage for the Jerusalem council's careful deliberation.
15:5.reflection: When other believers practice their faith differently than I do, do I assume the worst or seek understanding first?
15:5.action: Identify one believer whose practice differs from yours, and pray for wisdom to distinguish essential matters from cultural ones before discussing it.
15:5.prayer: Father, disagreements arise even among sincere believers. Guard me from demanding others conform to my traditions. Give me humility to weigh Scripture carefully and charity toward those who see things differently. Amen.

15:6.devotion: Rather than splitting over the dispute, the apostles and elders came together to consider the matter. The early church modeled a commitment to seeking God's will collectively through discussion, Scripture, and testimony instead of rushing to division or acting on impulse alone.
15:6.reflection: When conflict arises in my church family, do I work toward resolution or let frustration do the deciding for me?
15:6.action: If a disagreement is troubling you in your congregation, take one step toward it today: schedule a conversation or commit it to prayer with a trusted leader.
15:6.prayer: Lord, thank You for the example of leaders who gathered to seek Your truth together. Help Your church today face hard questions with patience, honesty, and unity rather than division. Amen.

15:7.devotion: After much dispute, Peter stood and recalled how God had chosen him years earlier to bring the gospel to the Gentiles. He pointed the council back to God's own initiative: Gentiles had heard the word through Peter's preaching and believed, long before anyone debated the requirements.
15:7.reflection: Do I remember God's past faithfulness when facing today's disagreements, or does every conflict make me forget what He has already shown me?
15:7.action: Write down one time God clearly worked in your past, and keep it where you can consult it when facing a current decision.
15:7.prayer: Father, like Peter, help me remember Your past faithfulness when new questions arise. You are the One who opens hearts to believe. Remind me of what You have already done, and anchor me in it. Amen.

15:8.devotion: Peter continued: God, who knows the heart, gave the Holy Spirit to Gentile believers just as He had to Jewish believers. God's own testimony about these converts was the Spirit Himself. What God had accepted by His inner knowledge, the church had no grounds to reject.
15:8.reflection: Am I willing to trust that God knows hearts I cannot see, including those of people I find unfamiliar or different?
15:8.action: Today, catch one judgmental thought about another person and replace it with a prayer asking God, who knows their heart, to work in both your lives.
15:8.prayer: God who knows every heart, thank You that You see truly what I only guess at. Teach me to honor Your judgment above my assumptions and to welcome those You have received. Amen.

15:9.devotion: Peter declared that God made no distinction between Jewish and Gentile believers, purifying their hearts by faith. Cleansing came not through heritage, ritual, or law-keeping, but through trust in God. Before God, both groups stood on the same ground, cleansed by the same faith.
15:9.reflection: Do I ever treat fellow believers as second-class members of God's family when God Himself has made no such distinction?
15:9.action: Reach out today to a believer whose background or culture differs from yours—send a message, share a meal, or offer encouragement as an equal in Christ.
